exercises.passage:
A. The fictional harbour of Selwick has kept a water-level diary for seventy years. For most of that period, a keeper read a painted staff beside the landing steps every morning. Each entry included the date, reading and keeper's initials. The diary served boat operators deciding when shallow channels might be usable. It was never intended to record every rise and fall within a day, and the keepers did not claim that a morning observation represented the daily maximum.

B. Recently, the harbour installed an electronic gauge that records a reading every fifteen minutes. Engineers left the painted staff in place and ran both systems together for six months. During this overlap, they noticed that the electronic readings were consistently four centimetres higher. An inspection revealed that the two devices used different reference points. Adjusting the electronic record to the old reference removed the constant difference; it did not remove the natural variation between readings taken at different times.

C. Digitising the handwritten diary created a separate difficulty. A mark resembling a seven sometimes meant a one in an earlier keeper's handwriting. Two volunteers independently transcribed every page, and a coordinator checked disagreements against the original. Blank cells were preserved as missing observations, rather than filled with estimates. Photographs of the pages remained linked to the digital entries so later users could reconsider uncertain readings without handling the fragile notebooks.

D. The combined record now supports a classroom project on change and uncertainty. Students can compare observations taken at the same time of day, but their teacher discourages direct comparisons between old daily readings and new daily maxima. The richer electronic record answers questions the diary cannot answer. Meanwhile, the diary extends the period available for a carefully defined comparison. The harbour has not yet published a calculation of the long-term trend. Its first priority is to explain how each part of the record was produced.
exercises.evidence: Each entry included the date, reading and keeper's initials.

exercises.prompt: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage. Complete the note: The electronic gauge records a reading every _____.

explanation.en: Fifteen minutes is the recording interval, not the overlap duration.
explanation.ru: Fifteen minutes — интервал записи, а не длительность совместной работы.

exercises.passage:
A. The fictional harbour of Selwick has kept a water-level diary for seventy years. For most of that period, a keeper read a painted staff beside the landing steps every morning. Each entry included the date, reading and keeper's initials. The diary served boat operators deciding when shallow channels might be usable. It was never intended to record every rise and fall within a day, and the keepers did not claim that a morning observation represented the daily maximum.

B. Recently, the harbour installed an electronic gauge that records a reading every fifteen minutes. Engineers left the painted staff in place and ran both systems together for six months. During this overlap, they noticed that the electronic readings were consistently four centimetres higher. An inspection revealed that the two devices used different reference points. Adjusting the electronic record to the old reference removed the constant difference; it did not remove the natural variation between readings taken at different times.

C. Digitising the handwritten diary created a separate difficulty. A mark resembling a seven sometimes meant a one in an earlier keeper's handwriting. Two volunteers independently transcribed every page, and a coordinator checked disagreements against the original. Blank cells were preserved as missing observations, rather than filled with estimates. Photographs of the pages remained linked to the digital entries so later users could reconsider uncertain readings without handling the fragile notebooks.

D. The combined record now supports a classroom project on change and uncertainty. Students can compare observations taken at the same time of day, but their teacher discourages direct comparisons between old daily readings and new daily maxima. The richer electronic record answers questions the diary cannot answer. Meanwhile, the diary extends the period available for a carefully defined comparison. The harbour has not yet published a calculation of the long-term trend. Its first priority is to explain how each part of the record was produced.
exercises.evidence: An inspection revealed that the two devices used different reference points.

exercises.passage:
A. A tool-lending library in the fictional district of Merrow began with donated drills, ladders and gardening equipment. Its organisers wanted residents to complete occasional household jobs without owning rarely used tools. Members paid an annual fee, but individual loans carried no additional charge. Before taking electrical equipment home, every borrower attended a safety demonstration. The organisers treated this requirement as part of the lending service, rather than assuming that familiar-looking tools were necessarily familiar to their users.

B. The first booking system listed tools by the order in which they had been donated. This made sense to the volunteers who remembered each donation, but new members struggled to find what they needed. A redesign grouped tools by activity, such as decorating or garden maintenance. It also displayed photographs beside the names. The number of available tools stayed the same, and the redesign did not extend opening hours. Its purpose was to make the existing collection easier to navigate.

C. Demand was uneven. Ladders were requested most often at weekends, while sewing machines were borrowed throughout the week. To reduce unsuccessful weekend visits, the library introduced reservations for ladders. A reservation held an item until noon on the agreed day; after that time, another member could borrow it. Equipment returned with a fault was placed on a separate shelf and checked before being offered again. Volunteers recorded repair work even when it required only a minor adjustment.

D. After one year, organisers surveyed members who had completed at least one loan. Many respondents said that borrowing encouraged them to attempt small repairs. However, the questionnaire did not ask whether respondents had bought fewer new products. The organisers therefore avoided claiming a measured reduction in household consumption. They also recognised that opinions from active borrowers might differ from those of members who had never borrowed. Their next survey will invite both groups and ask separately about convenience, confidence and purchasing decisions.

A. A tool-lending library in the fictional district of Merrow began with donated drills, ladders and gardening equipment. Its organisers wanted residents to complete occasional household jobs without owning rarely used tools. Members paid an annual fee, but individual loans carried no additional charge. exercises.author: StylishSAT original AI-authored draft, 2026-09-05; independent specialist review pending
exercises.passage:
A. In a teaching case set in fictional Bracken County, archivists compare three maps of the same rural area. A landowner's map shows estate boundaries and rentable fields. A walking club's map emphasises paths, springs and steep slopes. A transport map marks roads by the width of vehicles they can carry. All three maps are accurate for their stated purposes, yet they give very different impressions of which places matter. The exercise begins by asking students to identify each map's intended user.

B. A narrow path near Mill Wood appears on the walking map but not on the estate map. One student initially interprets its absence as proof that the path had not existed when the estate map was drawn. The archivist points out that the mapmaker was recording taxable land, not every route across it. Absence from a selective map cannot, by itself, establish absence on the ground. Students are asked to search for other records before dating the path.

C. A maintenance ledger supplies additional evidence. An entry describes replacing a small bridge where the path crosses a stream, several years before the estate map was produced. The entry supports the existence of a crossing at that time, although it says nothing about how often people used it. A later photograph shows the same bridge from an identifiable bend in the stream. Together, these sources make an earlier crossing more credible without revealing the path's full history.

D. For the final task, students create a map for people carrying heavy shopping bags. They include steps, steep gradients and places to rest, features that the transport map largely ignores. They must also state when each route was checked. A level-looking path can become difficult after rain, so a map useful in dry weather may offer misleading guidance in other conditions. The class concludes that useful mapping requires deliberate selection and clear limits. Adding every known feature would not automatically make a map easier to use; it could hide the information its audience actually needs.

exercises.author: StylishSAT original AI-authored draft, 2026-09-05; independent specialist review pending
exercises.passage:
A. The fictional Orlan music school converted a former assembly hall into a rehearsal room. Its smooth walls and bare floor made spoken instructions difficult to understand when several groups practised together. Staff could hear words continuing to reflect after a speaker had stopped. The renovation team described this persistence as reverberation. Their aim was to improve clarity inside the room, not to prevent all sound from passing into neighbouring rooms; the two problems required different kinds of investigation.

B. Rather than buy materials immediately, students tested removable fabric panels. They placed a loudspeaker at one marked position and a microphone at three listening positions. Every comparison used the same recorded sound and loudspeaker setting. The students measured how long the sound took to decay after the recording ended. Panels reduced this decay time at all three positions, although the reduction was smallest beside a large window. The exercise report did not contain any measurements from outside the room.

C. Location mattered as much as total panel area. When every panel was placed on the rear wall, musicians near the side walls still reported confusing reflections. Moving some panels to the sides improved those reports without adding more material. Yet covering every available surface was not the preferred solution. In a listening session, several musicians found the most heavily covered arrangement uncomfortably dull. They wanted enough reflected sound to hear their own instruments naturally while still distinguishing other players.

D. The final arrangement combined fixed wall panels with curtains that could be opened or closed. A small ensemble used a different curtain position from the full student orchestra. The school kept a diagram of successful arrangements beside the entrance, encouraging users to start with a suitable setting and adjust it after listening. Staff described the result as adaptable rather than perfect. A room that supports one activity can hinder another, and a single acoustic measurement cannot decide every musical preference. Future users will therefore evaluate the room through both repeatable tests and carefully described listening experiences.
exercises.evidence: The renovation team described this persistence as reverberation.

explanation.en: The stated aim concerns internal clarity, not complete isolation.

The renovation team described this persistence as reverberation. Their aim was to improve clarity inside the room, not to prevent all sound from passing into neighbouring rooms; the two problems required different kinds of investigation.

B. Rather than buy materials immediately, students tested removable fabric panels. They placed a loudspeaker at one marked position and a microphone at three listening positions. Every comparison used the same recorded sound and loudspeaker setting. The students measured how long the sound took to decay after the recording ended. Panels reduced this decay time at all three positions, although the reduction was smallest beside a large window. The exercise report did not contain any measurements from outside the room.

C. Location mattered as much as total panel area. When every panel was placed on the rear wall, musicians near the side walls still reported confusing reflections. Moving some panels to the sides improved those reports without adding more material. Yet covering every available surface was not the preferred solution. In a listening session, several musicians found the most heavily covered arrangement uncomfortably dull. They wanted enough reflected sound to hear their own instruments naturally while still distinguishing other players.

D. The final arrangement combined fixed wall panels with curtains that could be opened or closed. A small ensemble used a different curtain position from the full student orchestra. The school kept a diagram of successful arrangements beside the entrance, encouraging users to start with a suitable setting and adjust it after listening. Staff described the result as adaptable rather than perfect. A room that supports one activity can hinder another, and a single acoustic measurement cannot decide every musical preference. Future users will therefore evaluate the room through both repeatable tests and carefully described listening experiences.

exercises.passage:
A. In a fictional canal-management exercise, the town of Edrin must decide where to remove accumulated sediment. Boat owners report that one bend has become difficult to navigate, but the maintenance budget cannot cover the whole canal. Engineers begin by distinguishing water depth from sediment thickness. A shallow reading might result from a low water level as well as a high bed. Surveying without recording the water level could therefore direct expensive work to the wrong place.

B. The survey boat follows six fixed lines across the bend. Along each line, a sounding instrument records the distance between the water surface and the bed. Staff also read a water-level marker at the lock, allowing depths taken on different mornings to be compared against a common reference. The survey shows a raised deposit beside the inner bank. Samples from this deposit contain finer particles than samples from the main channel. The exercise provides no chemical analysis of either sample.

C. Removing the entire deposit would create a wide navigation route, but it would also remove a strip used by waterside plants. The engineers draw up a narrower option: clear a central passage while retaining most of the shallow edge. This proposal requires more precise marking before work starts. It also means the contractor cannot simply follow the visible bank. The marked route curves away from that bank in order to connect with deeper water on both sides of the bend.

D. The town chooses the narrower option for a trial season. After the work, surveyors repeat the original six lines instead of selecting new positions that merely look representative. Boats are asked to report where they still encounter difficulty, and the plant strip is photographed from fixed points. The town will assess navigation and habitat separately before judging the combined result. A single successful boat journey would not demonstrate that every vessel can pass safely, just as one photograph cannot describe all ecological change. The exercise presents maintenance as a decision supported by several kinds of evidence, with trade-offs that remain visible even after a practical solution is chosen.

exercises.passage:
A. In a fictional canal-management exercise, the town of Edrin must decide where to remove accumulated sediment. Boat owners report that one bend has become difficult to navigate, but the maintenance budget cannot cover the whole canal. Engineers begin by distinguishing water depth from sediment thickness. A shallow reading might result from a low water level as well as a high bed. Surveying without recording the water level could therefore direct expensive work to the wrong place.

B. The survey boat follows six fixed lines across the bend. Along each line, a sounding instrument records the distance between the water surface and the bed. Staff also read a water-level marker at the lock, allowing depths taken on different mornings to be compared against a common reference. The survey shows a raised deposit beside the inner bank. Samples from this deposit contain finer particles than samples from the main channel. The exercise provides no chemical analysis of either sample.

C. Removing the entire deposit would create a wide navigation route, but it would also remove a strip used by waterside plants. The engineers draw up a narrower option: clear a central passage while retaining most of the shallow edge. This proposal requires more precise marking before work starts. It also means the contractor cannot simply follow the visible bank. The marked route curves away from that bank in order to connect with deeper water on both sides of the bend.

D. The town chooses the narrower option for a trial season. After the work, surveyors repeat the original six lines instead of selecting new positions that merely look representative. Boats are asked to report where they still encounter difficulty, and the plant strip is photographed from fixed points. The town will assess navigation and habitat separately before judging the combined result. A single successful boat journey would not demonstrate that every vessel can pass safely, just as one photograph cannot describe all ecological change. The exercise presents maintenance as a decision supported by several kinds of evidence, with trade-offs that remain visible even after a practical solution is chosen.

exercises.passage:
A. A ceramics workshop in the fictional town of Neris uses broken test tiles to teach students how evidence can be preserved during production. Each tile begins as a small rectangle cut from the same batch of clay. Before firing, a student scratches a code into its underside. The code links the tile to a notebook entry describing the clay, glaze mixture and intended kiln position. Without this link, an attractive result might be difficult to reproduce, while an unsuccessful result would reveal little about its cause.

B. In one class exercise, students apply the same glaze to twelve tiles. Six are placed near the kiln door and six near the back. The controller displays one temperature, measured by a sensor in the upper chamber. The teacher warns that this display does not establish identical conditions throughout the kiln. After firing, the rear tiles appear darker than those near the door. This pattern makes position worth investigating, but it does not show which specific local condition caused the colour difference.

C. For the next firing, the students exchange the positions of two labelled sets and add small heat-work indicators beside them. These indicators respond to the combined effect of temperature and time. They cannot provide a complete temperature history, but they can reveal whether the two positions received different overall treatment. Students also record the cooling schedule because glaze appearance may change after the highest temperature has already been reached. The notebook therefore covers the whole cycle rather than ending when heating stops.

D. The workshop keeps both successful and unsuccessful tiles on numbered boards. A visitor might prefer a display containing only beautiful surfaces, but the teaching collection has another purpose. Cracks, bubbles and unexpected colours help students ask more precise questions before changing a recipe. One disappointing tile is not automatically evidence that a glaze mixture is unusable. The same mixture may behave differently with another clay body or firing schedule. By retaining labelled examples and their records, the workshop makes later comparisons possible without pretending that a single test explains every outcome.

exercises.passage:
A. In the fictional farming district of Avel, small vegetable growers once cooled produce in separate ageing stores. A cooperative proposed a shared cold room close to the packing shed. Its argument was practical: deliveries already passed through that site, and trained staff could maintain one larger installation. The proposal did not assume that every crop should receive the same treatment. Growers supplied crop lists before designers chose the room's operating range and divided its interior into storage zones.

B. A pilot compared the electricity used by the new room with the combined use of the old stores over a four-week harvest period. The new room used less electricity in total, but it also held a smaller mass of produce. Dividing electricity use by the mass stored reversed the apparent advantage. The cooperative's report therefore presented both totals and use per kilogram. Neither measure alone answered every question: the total mattered for the electricity bill, while the ratio helped compare storage efficiency.

C. Staff discovered another problem during busy afternoons. The main door was repeatedly left open while crates were sorted outside. They introduced a staging area where complete loads could be prepared before the door opened. A door alarm sounded after a set interval, but the team treated it as a reminder rather than a substitute for organising work. The revised routine reduced open-door time in a second observation week. That week had cooler weather, so its electricity result could not be attributed solely to the new routine.

D. Members disagreed about charging. A flat fee was simple, yet growers using little space considered it unfair. Charging only by crate count ignored the fact that some crops remained for much longer than others. The cooperative eventually adopted a charge based on occupied space and storage duration, with a separate membership contribution for fixed costs. This arrangement required more record keeping than the original proposal. Members accepted that burden because the records made bills easier to explain. The case illustrates how technical performance, daily routines and payment rules can all determine whether shared equipment proves useful.

exercises.passage:
A. In the fictional farming district of Avel, small vegetable growers once cooled produce in separate ageing stores. A cooperative proposed a shared cold room close to the packing shed. Its argument was practical: deliveries already passed through that site, and trained staff could maintain one larger installation. The proposal did not assume that every crop should receive the same treatment. Growers supplied crop lists before designers chose the room's operating range and divided its interior into storage zones.

B. A pilot compared the electricity used by the new room with the combined use of the old stores over a four-week harvest period. The new room used less electricity in total, but it also held a smaller mass of produce. Dividing electricity use by the mass stored reversed the apparent advantage. The cooperative's report therefore presented both totals and use per kilogram. Neither measure alone answered every question: the total mattered for the electricity bill, while the ratio helped compare storage efficiency.

C. Staff discovered another problem during busy afternoons. The main door was repeatedly left open while crates were sorted outside. They introduced a staging area where complete loads could be prepared before the door opened. A door alarm sounded after a set interval, but the team treated it as a reminder rather than a substitute for organising work. The revised routine reduced open-door time in a second observation week. That week had cooler weather, so its electricity result could not be attributed solely to the new routine.

D. Members disagreed about charging. A flat fee was simple, yet growers using little space considered it unfair. Charging only by crate count ignored the fact that some crops remained for much longer than others. The cooperative eventually adopted a charge based on occupied space and storage duration, with a separate membership contribution for fixed costs. This arrangement required more record keeping than the original proposal. Members accepted that burden because the records made bills easier to explain. The case illustrates how technical performance, daily routines and payment rules can all determine whether shared equipment proves useful.
exercises.evidence: A flat fee was simple, yet growers using little space considered it unfair.

exercises.author: StylishSAT original AI-authored draft, 2026-09-05; independent specialist review pending
exercises.passage:
A. A nature reserve in the fictional valley of Ossel receives many visitors along a wetland trail. During rainy months, walkers step around muddy sections and gradually widen the route. Managers consider a raised boardwalk, but they do not regard construction as an automatic ecological improvement. Building supports, transporting timber and concentrating visitors can all affect the site. Before choosing a design, the reserve team maps existing damage and identifies areas that should remain undisturbed.

B. Three route options are drawn. The shortest crosses a patch where water remains visible late into summer. A second follows the old footpath but requires several sharp turns. The third is longer and reaches a firmer ridge before returning to the viewing point. Staff choose the third route for detailed assessment because materials can be brought along the ridge without driving across the wettest ground. This choice concerns access during construction as well as the experience of future walkers.

C. A trial section uses gaps between the boards to allow rain and light through. The gaps must also be narrow enough for the mobility aids tested by the visitor group. Handrails are added where the platform rises higher above the ground, but not along every metre. The team records the reasons for these differences on the design drawing. A uniform appearance would be simpler to explain, yet the drawing shows that different stretches present different practical needs.

D. After opening, volunteers count walkers from a fixed observation point and photograph the adjacent vegetation. Fewer people leave the new path than left the old muddy trail during the recorded visits. However, the counts cover only daylight hours, and the team has no measurements of night-time use. Managers also note that reduced trampling beside the boardwalk cannot establish recovery across the whole wetland. Their report separates visitor behaviour, local plant cover and broader habitat conditions. They plan to repeat observations in another wet season, when the old route had previously been most difficult. The boardwalk is therefore treated as a monitored intervention whose benefits and limitations require continued observation.
exercises.evidence: During rainy months, walkers step around muddy sections and gradually widen the route.

explanation.en: The passage explicitly rejects automatic improvement.

exercises.passage:
A. The fictional Dalen transport museum commissions a tactile map for visitors who explore information through touch. Its existing printed plan contains thin lines, closely spaced labels and decorative details. Simply raising every printed feature would create a crowded surface. The designer therefore begins with the visitor's main decisions: locating the entrance, finding the central hall and choosing a route to the lifts. This priority list determines which features appear on the first prototype.

B. Raised paths connect important destinations, while separate textures distinguish indoor galleries from the outdoor courtyard. The prototype uses large symbols whose meanings are explained in a key at the lower edge. A small orientation mark indicates the entrance side. During testing, participants are asked to trace a journey rather than merely name isolated symbols. A symbol may be recognisable on its own yet difficult to locate among neighbouring features, so successful identification does not guarantee successful navigation.

C. The first trials reveal a problem near the café. Two routes pass so close together that several participants treat them as a single path. Increasing their separation solves this confusion, even though it makes the tactile layout less geometrically faithful to the building. The designer records the adjustment as deliberate exaggeration. Distances on this map are not intended for measurement; connections and relative positions are more important for the journeys being supported.

D. The map is installed beside an audio description, with a short instruction inviting visitors to begin at the orientation mark. Museum staff keep the printed plan available as another format. No single presentation is assumed to suit every person or every task. The project report describes the prototype sessions in detail but does not compare total visit duration before and after installation. Its strongest evidence concerns whether particular routes could be followed during the tests. The museum plans to revise the map when gallery entrances change, because an accessible format can still become misleading if its information is outdated. Accessibility is thus treated as a continuing relationship between design, content and the visitor's purpose.
exercises.evidence: The designer therefore begins with the visitor's main decisions: locating the entrance, finding the central hall and choosing a route to the lifts.

A. The fictional Dalen transport museum commissions a tactile map for visitors who explore information through touch. Its existing printed plan contains thin lines, closely spaced labels and decorative details. Simply raising every printed feature would create a crowded surface. The designer therefore begins with the visitor's main decisions: locating the entrance, finding the central hall and choosing a route to the lifts. This priority list determines which features appear on the first prototype.

B. Raised paths connect important destinations, while separate textures distinguish indoor galleries from the outdoor courtyard. The prototype uses large symbols whose meanings are explained in a key at the lower edge. A small orientation mark indicates the entrance side. During testing, participants are asked to trace a journey rather than merely name isolated symbols. A symbol may be recognisable on its own yet difficult to locate among neighbouring features, so successful identification does not guarantee successful navigation.

C. The first trials reveal a problem near the café. Two routes pass so close together that several participants treat them as a single path. Increasing their separation solves this confusion, even though it makes the tactile layout less geometrically faithful to the building. The designer records the adjustment as deliberate exaggeration. Distances on this map are not intended for measurement; connections and relative positions are more important for the journeys being supported.

D. The map is installed beside an audio description, with a short instruction inviting visitors to begin at the orientation mark. Museum staff keep the printed plan available as another format. No single presentation is assumed to suit every person or every task. The project report describes the prototype sessions in detail but does not compare total visit duration before and after installation. Its strongest evidence concerns whether particular routes could be followed during the tests. The museum plans to revise the map when gallery entrances change, because an accessible format can still become misleading if its information is outdated. Accessibility is thus treated as a continuing relationship between design, content and the visitor's purpose.
exercises.evidence: The project report describes the prototype sessions in detail but does not compare total visit duration before and after installation.

exercises.prompt: Choose ONE answer. Which conclusion follows from the planned revisions?
options: Accessible information must stay current as the building changes
One format is sufficient for every visitor
Only the physical format needs updating
acceptedAnswers: Accessible information must stay current as the building changes

explanation.en: Accessibility includes accurate current content.
explanation.ru: Доступность включает точное актуальное содержание.

hints.ru: Сопоставьте весь смысл каждого варианта с доказательством, учитывая ограничения.

exercises.passage:
A. In the fictional city of Lureth, a school network runs an exercise on observing flower visitors. Pupils want to compare a frequently mown lawn with a nearby strip allowed to flower. Their teacher first distinguishes visits from individual insects. One insect may return several times, and without identifying it reliably the observers cannot know whether repeated visits represent different animals. The recording sheet therefore asks for flower visits, not a count of the local insect population.

B. Each class observes a marked square for ten minutes. A visit is counted when an insect lands on an open flower; flying over the square does not qualify. Groups use the same definition and practise with a short video before visiting the sites. They also record cloud cover and whether strong wind interrupts observation. The exercise avoids asking beginners to identify every species. Instead, pupils sort visitors into a few broad groups illustrated on their recording cards.

C. Initial results show more visits in the flowering strip, but most lawn observations were made on a colder morning. The teacher asks the pupils to explain why that difference matters before drawing a conclusion about mowing. On the next round, paired groups observe both sites at the same time. The flowering strip again records more visits during those sessions. This strengthens the site comparison, although the two locations still differ in other ways, including their distance from a hedge.

D. The pupils prepare a display showing every session rather than only the largest difference. One windy session has very few recorded visits at either site. They retain it with a note instead of deleting an inconvenient result. Their conclusion is limited to the observations made: under the recorded conditions, the flowering strip received more visits. They do not claim that the strip increased insect breeding or that every unmown space would produce the same result. The exercise report contains no observations of nests or young insects. Its educational value lies partly in learning to define a measurement, make a fairer comparison and explain what the resulting numbers can and cannot establish.
exercises.evidence: The recording sheet therefore asks for flower visits, not a count of the local insect population.

exercises.prompt: Decide whether the statement agrees with the passage. Choose TRUE, FALSE, or NOT GIVEN: An insect must land on an open flower to count as a visit.

explanation.en: The operational definition requires landing; flying over does not qualify.
explanation.ru: Рабочее определение требует посадки; пролёт не засчитывается.

hints.ru: Найдите нужное обсуждение в абзаце B.

typicalErrors.ru: Пропуск прямого соответствия из-за перефразирования текста в вопросе.

exercises.passage:
A. In the fictional city of Lureth, a school network runs an exercise on observing flower visitors. Pupils want to compare a frequently mown lawn with a nearby strip allowed to flower. Their teacher first distinguishes visits from individual insects. One insect may return several times, and without identifying it reliably the observers cannot know whether repeated visits represent different animals. The recording sheet therefore asks for flower visits, not a count of the local insect population.

B. Each class observes a marked square for ten minutes. A visit is counted when an insect lands on an open flower; flying over the square does not qualify. Groups use the same definition and practise with a short video before visiting the sites. They also record cloud cover and whether strong wind interrupts observation. The exercise avoids asking beginners to identify every species. Instead, pupils sort visitors into a few broad groups illustrated on their recording cards.

C. Initial results show more visits in the flowering strip, but most lawn observations were made on a colder morning. The teacher asks the pupils to explain why that difference matters before drawing a conclusion about mowing. On the next round, paired groups observe both sites at the same time. The flowering strip again records more visits during those sessions. This strengthens the site comparison, although the two locations still differ in other ways, including their distance from a hedge.

D. The pupils prepare a display showing every session rather than only the largest difference. One windy session has very few recorded visits at either site. They retain it with a note instead of deleting an inconvenient result. Their conclusion is limited to the observations made: under the recorded conditions, the flowering strip received more visits. They do not claim that the strip increased insect breeding or that every unmown space would produce the same result. The exercise report contains no observations of nests or young insects. Its educational value lies partly in learning to define a measurement, make a fairer comparison and explain what the resulting numbers can and cannot establish.

Comparing the pieces gives a reference for colour change under that particular exposure. The window trial does not represent every possible lighting condition, nor does it measure resistance to washing. The final display presents the recipe, treatment record and both pieces together. Visitors can therefore judge an initial colour alongside evidence about its later appearance. A caption naming a particular strike could steer a speaker towards that event even when the photograph evokes another occasion. A speaker may discuss casual employment without using that phrase, so an empty search result is not proof that the topic is absent. Users must therefore avoid treating the interview collection as a statistical sample of all former port workers. exercises.author: StylishSAT original AI-authored draft, 2026-09-05; independent specialist review pending
exercises.passage:
A. A delivery cooperative in the fictional city of Tivor tests cargo bicycles for a compact shopping district. The trial concerns the final stage of delivery, from a local depot to customers, rather than the complete journey from a factory. Parcels arrive at the depot in ordinary vans and are sorted into bicycle loads. The cooperative expects bicycles to be useful where narrow streets and scarce parking slow larger vehicles, but it does not assume they can carry every item.

B. Before the trial, dispatchers classify parcels by mass, dimensions and handling requirements. Fragile goods needing a special frame remain with the van service, even when they are light. The bicycle routes include only parcels that fit the approved boxes. Riders can make several trips during a shift, returning to the depot between loads. Consequently, the number of parcels carried at one time is different from the number delivered over the whole day.

C. The team compares completed deliveries per working hour for bicycles and vans on matched routes. Waiting time, loading and unsuccessful visits are included. Counting only time spent moving would favour whichever vehicle required more unrecorded preparation. On the selected routes, bicycles complete more deliveries per hour during the busiest traffic period. Outside that period, the difference is smaller. The report does not present a comparison for steep outer suburbs or for very large parcels.

D. Customers are offered a two-hour delivery window and can leave instructions for an authorised recipient. When nobody is available, the parcel returns to the depot; riders do not leave it in an unsecured doorway. The cooperative tracks these failed visits separately from vehicle delays. An efficient bicycle cannot solve a problem caused by missing access information. At the end of the trial, managers recommend keeping both bicycles and vans, assigning work according to route and load. They also retain the full journey in environmental accounting, including the vans that supply the depot. A successful final-stage experiment would be misleading if its report made the earlier transport disappear simply because it occurred outside the trial area.
exercises.evidence: The trial concerns the final stage of delivery, from a local depot to customers, rather than the complete journey from a factory.

A. Students at the fictional Rellin field school build a tabletop model of a mountain glacier. They use a slow-moving mixture in a transparent trough, adding material at the upper end and allowing it to leave at the lower end. The model is intended to demonstrate the balance between input and loss. It does not reproduce the complete behaviour of natural ice. The teacher begins by listing both the process represented and the features deliberately excluded.

B. Coloured bands are inserted across the mixture at regular intervals. As the material moves down the trough, the bands bend because the centre moves differently from the edges. Students sketch the changing pattern from above and photograph it through the side. A mark on the trough itself stays fixed, providing a reference against which movement can be judged. Without a stationary reference, a camera that shifted between photographs could create an apparent change unrelated to the model.

C. In the first run, the amount added matches the amount removed. The lower end remains approximately in the same place even though material continues to pass through the trough. This surprises students who equate an unchanged outline with no movement. In a second run, the input is reduced while removal continues at the original rate. After a delay, the lower end retreats. The delay matters: the outline responds to an imbalance over time rather than instantly displaying the latest input.

D. Students are then asked what the experiment can support. It illustrates how movement and overall size can change independently, and why a response may lag behind a change in supply. It cannot establish the speed of a real glacier by converting centimetres in the trough directly into kilometres in a valley. The mixture and natural ice have not been shown to obey an appropriate scaling relationship. The class report also contains no measurements of actual mountain snowfall. Instead of treating these limitations as failures, students use them to formulate the next questions. A model becomes more useful when its claims are tied to the mechanism it represents and kept separate from quantities it was never designed to predict.
exercises.evidence: They use a slow-moving mixture in a transparent trough, adding material at the upper end and allowing it to leave at the lower end.

options: Actual snowfall in a mountain range
The temperature of a glacier lake

explanation.en: Its purpose is a process relationship, not complete imitation.

exercises.passage:
A. The fictional town of Veyra reviews lighting along a riverside pedestrian route. Residents value seeing steps and other walkers, but some complain that bright lamps shine into bedroom windows. The council's design brief separates useful light on the path from unwanted light outside it. The aim is not simply to maximise brightness. A brighter installation could still make a route harder to use if direct glare prevents people from seeing darker areas ahead.

B. Designers test two fixtures on adjacent sections. Both use the same type of lamp, but one fixture directs more light downwards through a shield. Measurements are taken at marked points on the path and at a nearby building façade. The shielded fixture produces lower readings at the façade while maintaining the specified path illumination. This result concerns the tested geometry; the designers do not assume the same fixture will perform identically at every mounting height or distance.

C. Volunteers walk the test sections after their eyes have adjusted to outdoor conditions. They are asked to identify a low step and describe any uncomfortable glare. The order of the sections is reversed for half the group, reducing the chance that always seeing one design first shapes the comparison. Participants generally prefer the shielded section, although several request clearer marking on the step itself. The council treats that request as a surface-design issue as well as a lighting issue.

D. The final proposal combines shielded lamps with contrasting step edges and a lower overnight setting during hours of reduced use. The council leaves the route open throughout the night. It plans to check whether walkers still identify obstacles at the lower setting before adopting it permanently. The trial report does not measure changes in sleep quality in nearby homes. exercises.passage:
A. A manuscript seminar at the fictional Eliston library studies handwritten notes in the margins of an old geography book. The printed text describes routes between trading towns, but later readers have added prices, corrections and occasional drawings. The librarian asks students to treat the volume as evidence of repeated use. Its margins may reveal how people engaged with the book, even when those readers left no separate account of their lives.

B. Students first separate observations from interpretations. They can see that a note crosses a printed border and that its ink is paler than the ink of a neighbouring note. They cannot date it precisely from colour alone. Ink composition, light exposure and storage conditions can all affect appearance. A date written beside a note might refer to the event being described rather than the moment of writing. The seminar therefore avoids arranging every annotation into a confident timeline.

C. One reader has replaced a printed distance with a shorter figure and added the phrase by the new bridge. A municipal account elsewhere in the collection records payment for building a bridge on that route. This connection provides a possible context for the correction. It does not identify the reader, and it does not prove that the reader personally crossed the bridge. The librarian encourages students to state the strength of the link accurately: two sources describe a related change, but important details remain unknown.

D. For a digital exhibition, students photograph whole pages before making close-up images of individual notes. Cropping too tightly could conceal whether a comment belongs to the main text, a map or another reader's annotation. The exhibition allows viewers to move from each detail back to its page. Transcriptions retain crossed-out words where they remain legible, and uncertain letters are marked rather than silently guessed. The resulting display is less tidy than a clean rewritten text, but it preserves the evidence behind the interpretation. The seminar concludes that signs of use are not merely damage to be ignored. They can become historical sources when their physical relationships and uncertainties remain available for other readers to inspect.

exercises.passage:
A. In the fictional district of Harven, a farming college tests methods for storing a small grain harvest. The exercise begins after threshing, when the grain has been separated from the stalks but still needs preparation for storage. Students measure moisture before placing grain in containers. Their teacher warns that a tightly closed container is not a substitute for suitable initial drying. The trial compares storage arrangements only after the batches meet the same starting moisture requirement.

B. The students divide one mixed batch into equal portions and place them in three types of container. Every container receives a label with its starting mass and date. The storage room has warmer shelves near a sunlit wall and cooler shelves on the opposite side. To prevent container type from being confused with shelf location, each type is represented on both sides. Students also rotate the positions according to a written schedule, recording each move.

C. Inspection uses a fixed procedure. A sample is removed from each container at the same interval, weighed and examined for visible damage. The removed sample is not returned to storage. Its mass is recorded so that later comparisons can account for grain deliberately taken out. Without that correction, a container sampled more heavily could appear to have suffered greater unexplained loss. The exercise distinguishes measured change from an accounting mistake.

D. At the end of the trial, one container type has the smallest adjusted mass loss, but it is also the most expensive to buy. Students calculate its extra cost for the quantity actually stored, rather than assuming that a result from small containers transfers directly to a commercial warehouse. The report contains no measurements of the grain's vitamin content. Appearance and retained mass therefore cannot establish nutritional superiority. For their recommendation, students present storage loss, purchase cost and practical handling separately. A grower with limited cash may weigh those factors differently from a cooperative storing a larger harvest. The class concludes that a technically promising result becomes useful advice only when the comparison, its scale and the decision-maker's constraints are made clear.

A. In the fictional district of Harven, a farming college tests methods for storing a small grain harvest. The exercise begins after threshing, when the grain has been separated from the stalks but still needs preparation for storage. Students measure moisture before placing grain in containers. Their teacher warns that a tightly closed container is not a substitute for suitable initial drying. The trial compares storage arrangements only after the batches meet the same starting moisture requirement.

B. The students divide one mixed batch into equal portions and place them in three types of container. Every container receives a label with its starting mass and date. The storage room has warmer shelves near a sunlit wall and cooler shelves on the opposite side. To prevent container type from being confused with shelf location, each type is represented on both sides. Students also rotate the positions according to a written schedule, recording each move.

Its mass is recorded so that later comparisons can account for grain deliberately taken out. Without that correction, a container sampled more heavily could appear to have suffered greater unexplained loss. The exercise distinguishes measured change from an accounting mistake.

D. At the end of the trial, one container type has the smallest adjusted mass loss, but it is also the most expensive to buy. Students calculate its extra cost for the quantity actually stored, rather than assuming that a result from small containers transfers directly to a commercial warehouse. The report contains no measurements of the grain's vitamin content. Appearance and retained mass therefore cannot establish nutritional superiority. For their recommendation, students present storage loss, purchase cost and practical handling separately. A grower with limited cash may weigh those factors differently from a cooperative storing a larger harvest. The class concludes that a technically promising result becomes useful advice only when the comparison, its scale and the decision-maker's constraints are made clear.

exercises.passage:
A. In a river-planning exercise set in fictional Corven, a low barrier once diverted water towards a mill. The mill has closed, but the barrier remains. Residents disagree about removing it: some want a more continuous channel, while others value the pool above it. The planning team begins by mapping present uses rather than assuming that an obsolete industrial structure has no current significance. Anglers, walkers and a nearby landowner are invited to describe how they use the site.

B. Surveyors measure the bed above and below the barrier and take sediment samples from several depths. A thick layer of fine material has accumulated upstream. Removing the structure could allow some of this material to move downstream, so the proposal must consider more than the concrete alone. The exercise does not provide chemical tests of the sediment. Students cannot classify it as either contaminated or uncontaminated on the basis of its colour or grain size.

C. One proposal removes the barrier in a single operation. Another lowers it in stages, surveying the channel between stages. The staged option takes longer and requires repeated site visits, but it may reveal how the river responds before the next change is made. It is not presented as risk-free. A response observed after the first lowering may differ from the response after the final section is removed, especially if water flow changes between visits.

D. The planning team defines several outcomes before work starts. These include water levels beside the landowner's field, changes in the upstream pool and continuity of the channel. Photographs will be taken from fixed positions, and survey sections will be repeated at recorded water levels. The team also plans observations after a high-flow event, because a calm period may reveal little about sediment movement. Its report does not predict that every fish species will increase after removal. Instead, it sets out what will be measured and when the decision should be reconsidered. The case presents restoration as a change whose consequences must be examined at the site, with public preferences and physical processes both contributing to the choice.

exercises.passage:
A. In a fictional coastal-planning study, the town of Caldrin considers moving a flood embankment inland and allowing tidal water into a low field. Supporters describe the resulting area as a possible salt marsh, while opponents ask whether the existing grazing land can be replaced. The study separates three questions: what landform might develop, how water would move, and who would bear the change in land use. Answering one of these questions would not settle the others.

B. Surveyors discover that the field is lower than a nearby established marsh. A drawing that simply colours the field green therefore conceals an important difference. The field may first become open water or bare sediment rather than immediately supporting the same vegetation as its neighbour. To investigate this possibility, the team measures surface height along a grid and compares it with recorded tidal levels. The exercise describes potential development, not a promise that the new site will reproduce the old marsh.

C. A computer model tests two widths of opening in the old embankment. The wider opening fills and drains the field more quickly under the modelled conditions. However, the team does not interpret faster exchange as automatically better. It may alter sediment transport as well as water timing. The model assumes the opening retains its designed shape; it does not calculate how erosion might enlarge it. Engineers therefore identify maintenance of the opening as a separate question that the initial simulation cannot resolve.

D. The proposed trial includes height markers, water-level sensors and photographs from fixed stations. Grazing losses are recorded in a separate account rather than offset by an invented monetary value for future wildlife. The planning report supplies no survey of breeding birds, because tidal entry has not begun. Residents are shown several possible trajectories, each linked to stated assumptions and observations that would support reconsideration. The report's cautious language does not mean the project has no purpose. It means that a desired outcome, a simulated response and an observed result occupy different stages of reasoning. The council must choose whether the expected benefits justify a trial while remaining prepared to alter the design if the developing site contradicts its assumptions.
exercises.evidence: The study separates three questions: what landform might develop, how water would move, and who would bear the change in land use.

exercises.passage:
A. The fictional transport authority of Istren plans an express bus linking three outer neighbourhoods with a railway station. Planners use existing ticket records to estimate possible demand, but the records contain only journeys made on current services. People who avoid those services because they are slow or inconvenient do not appear as potential passengers in the same way. Historical use provides a starting point, not a complete picture of demand for a different service.

B. A household questionnaire asks residents how often they would use an express bus under a specified timetable and fare. The planners keep those conditions visible in the question because enthusiasm for an undefined improvement is difficult to translate into a forecast. Responses still represent intentions rather than observed journeys. Some residents may overestimate future use, while others may not yet recognise occasions when the new service would be helpful. The authority therefore reports a range instead of treating every positive response as a guaranteed daily boarding.

C. The initial forecast combines current passenger transfers with estimated new trips. Analysts remove transfers that would merely shift between stops on the same express route, avoiding counting the same person twice. They publish separate estimates for weekday mornings and the rest of the week. A strong morning peak does not necessarily support frequent departures throughout the day. The operating plan must account for where and when demand occurs, not only the weekly total.

D. A twelve-week trial follows. Automatic counters record boardings, while short interviews ask whether a journey replaced another bus trip, a car trip or no previous trip. The counters cannot answer that substitution question by themselves. During the first fortnight, travel is free; subsequent weeks use the proposed fare. Analysts keep these periods separate when comparing observations with the original priced-service forecast. The trial report does not describe passenger numbers during the winter holidays, which fall outside the trial. At the review meeting, the authority considers timing changes before deciding whether to expand the route. Forecasting is presented as a sequence of explicit assumptions, observation and revision, rather than a single number that becomes authoritative merely because it was produced by a detailed calculation.

exercises.author: StylishSAT original AI-authored draft, 2026-09-05; independent specialist review pending
exercises.passage:
A. In a fictional archaeology teaching collection, excavators recover glass beads from two areas of a former settlement. One group comes from a workshop floor and another from a burial several streets away. Their similar blue colour suggests a possible relationship, but the project director warns that appearance alone cannot establish a shared place of manufacture. The teaching exercise asks students to build an argument from several kinds of evidence while keeping the original recovery contexts distinct.

B. Microscopic examination reveals a small hole running through every bead. Several workshop examples also carry irregular glass trails around their openings, whereas the burial examples have smoother ends. These observations are consistent with different stages of finishing. They do not prove that the rough examples were rejected products; unfinished items might have been awaiting further work when they were left on the floor. Students record the visible features before assigning a production label.

C. Chemical measurements show that most beads in both groups share a similar pattern of selected elements. Two workshop beads differ from that pattern. The analysts retain these exceptions in the table rather than reporting only a group average. Similar composition supports compatibility with a common material source, but it cannot identify an individual craftsperson. Nor does it prove that every bead was made at the excavated workshop. Glass material could have moved between workshops before being shaped into finished objects.

D. The burial also contains a metal clasp whose position was carefully recorded. Its association helps describe how the beads were deposited, but the exercise supplies no inscription naming the person buried there. A drawing reconstructing a necklace is therefore labelled as one possible arrangement. The students' final report places find locations, surface observations and chemical results in separate sections before explaining where their implications overlap. Its strongest conclusion is narrower than the first visual impression: some evidence links the groups, while production location, maker identity and final arrangement remain uncertain. The director regards this restraint as a positive result. A persuasive reconstruction does not require every blank to be filled; it requires readers to see which connections are observed, which are inferred and which have not yet been established.

exercises.passage:
A. In a fictional archaeology teaching collection, excavators recover glass beads from two areas of a former settlement. One group comes from a workshop floor and another from a burial several streets away. Their similar blue colour suggests a possible relationship, but the project director warns that appearance alone cannot establish a shared place of manufacture. The teaching exercise asks students to build an argument from several kinds of evidence while keeping the original recovery contexts distinct.

B. Microscopic examination reveals a small hole running through every bead. Several workshop examples also carry irregular glass trails around their openings, whereas the burial examples have smoother ends. These observations are consistent with different stages of finishing. They do not prove that the rough examples were rejected products; unfinished items might have been awaiting further work when they were left on the floor. Students record the visible features before assigning a production label.

C. Chemical measurements show that most beads in both groups share a similar pattern of selected elements. Two workshop beads differ from that pattern. The analysts retain these exceptions in the table rather than reporting only a group average. Similar composition supports compatibility with a common material source, but it cannot identify an individual craftsperson. Nor does it prove that every bead was made at the excavated workshop. Glass material could have moved between workshops before being shaped into finished objects.

D. The burial also contains a metal clasp whose position was carefully recorded. Its association helps describe how the beads were deposited, but the exercise supplies no inscription naming the person buried there. A drawing reconstructing a necklace is therefore labelled as one possible arrangement. The students' final report places find locations, surface observations and chemical results in separate sections before explaining where their implications overlap. Its strongest conclusion is narrower than the first visual impression: some evidence links the groups, while production location, maker identity and final arrangement remain uncertain. The director regards this restraint as a positive result. A persuasive reconstruction does not require every blank to be filled; it requires readers to see which connections are observed, which are inferred and which have not yet been established.

exercises.transcript: Good morning, and welcome to Lakeside Library. This is a synthetic practice conversation. I understand that you have moved into the neighbourhood and would like a borrowing card. We issue new cards at the information desk, just beside the entrance. Yes, I arrived last week and I am staying with my sister while I find a flat. My name is Elena Morris. I have brought my passport because the website says applicants must show identification, even if they already use another library. That is suitable for identification. We also need evidence of your current address. A recent bank statement will do; a travel ticket will not. You can display the statement on your phone, so there is no need to print it. I can show you that now. I had expected an annual charge of fifteen pounds because that appeared in an old leaflet. Your current notice says membership is free, although replacing a lost card may still involve a separate charge. You have read the correct notice. With your new card, you can borrow eight books at a time. Magazines do not count towards that total because they stay in the building. Downloadable material has its own separate allowance in the application. Eight will be plenty for me. I usually read one novel during the week and something about history at weekends. I see that books are normally loaned for three weeks, which should give me enough time to finish both types. If nobody has reserved a book, you may renew it through our website. Calling the building is unnecessary, and the self-service machines do not handle renewals. Please check your online account after submitting the request to make sure the new date appears. That sounds straightforward. I also need a quiet place for an online interview next month. I noticed a room labelled Cedar on the floor plan. The larger Maple room looks useful for groups, but Cedar seems the right size for one person. Cedar can be reserved in advance for up to two hours. Reservations open seven days before the date you need. Please bring your own headphones because sound from computer speakers would disturb readers using the desks immediately outside the room. Thank you. Before I leave, I will collect the card and check the opening hours. I had planned to return on Sunday, but I see the library is closed then. I will come on Monday instead, when the building opens again.

exercises.transcript: Welcome to the community recycling centre. This is a synthetic practice recording for new volunteers. Today we will concentrate on the sorting area rather than collection rounds. Before entering that area, please collect a yellow vest from the cupboard beside reception. You should already have received a short timetable. It places the safety briefing in the office, but that room is too small for our group. The briefing will actually take place in the courtyard, where everyone can see the equipment demonstration. We begin sorting at half past nine. The delivery vehicle arrives earlier, but only trained staff unload it. Please do not start moving containers while they are working. Once the engine is off, the supervisor will invite volunteers into the covered sorting space. The first table is for clean paper. Remove plastic sleeves before placing documents there, but leave ordinary metal staples attached because our processing equipment can remove them later. Wet paper belongs in a different container and should never be mixed with the dry material. Glass is handled in the next section. We separate bottles according to colour rather than size, because the receiving factory processes clear glass independently. You will find examples above each container. If you cannot identify a colour confidently, ask before placing the bottle anywhere. The metal station accepts drinks cans and food tins. Please leave the large pieces of machinery where staff have placed them. Those objects require a separate assessment, and volunteers should not try to dismantle them, even if they recognise the type of machine. You may find small batteries among donated objects. Put these in the red box beside the supervisor’s desk, not in the general metal container. The box remains indoors throughout the day so the collection team can account for its contents at closing time. We take a break at eleven, and there is drinking water in the kitchen. Bring your own cup if possible. Cups can also be borrowed, but they must be washed before you leave. Food should be eaten in the kitchen, away from the sorting tables. At the end of your shift, record the number of full containers on the clipboard. We are counting containers rather than weighing their contents today. Keep the counts for paper, glass, and metal separate so the office can arrange suitable transport for each material. Finally, return your vest to the same cupboard and sign out at reception. The next volunteer session is on Wednesday. A previous message said Tuesday, but a maintenance visit now occupies that morning. Your coordinator will send a reminder with the corrected day this afternoon.

exercises.transcript: Welcome to the Harbour Gallery. This is a synthetic practice recording introducing a fictional exhibition. The photographs you will see today document ordinary working spaces in our town. Rather than famous monuments, the photographer chose kitchens, workshops, and small offices that visitors normally never enter. Please begin in the blue room on your right. The printed map calls it the green room because the walls were repainted after the map was produced. We have placed a temporary sign at the doorway so that nobody follows the outdated colour description by mistake. The first sequence was photographed at dawn, before most employees arrived. That timing allowed the photographer to show how light moves across empty rooms. It also avoided interrupting anyone at work, although avoiding interruption was not the main artistic reason for choosing the early hour. Some visitors assume these images were taken with a phone. In fact, the photographer used a film camera for the entire project. Working with a limited number of exposures encouraged careful decisions about position and timing instead of taking many nearly identical photographs in quick succession. You will notice a short quotation below each photograph. These words come from interviews with the people who use the room, rather than comments written by the photographer. Reading them after viewing the image can change what you notice about an object near the edge of the frame. At the end of the first room, a table holds contact sheets. They display small versions of several exposures together. You asked about the room on Market Street, but someone reserved it this morning. We still have a room on Willow Road, close to the same bus route. Willow Road could work well for me. That is fine, because I do not have much luggage to carry upstairs. The rent is five hundred and forty pounds per month. That includes water and heating, but electricity is paid separately according to the meter. Internet access is included as well. We explain the separate electricity arrangement in the contract so there should be no surprise after you move in. That arrangement seems reasonable. The photograph shows a desk, which I will need for reading. I do not see a chair beside it, though. According to the written description, the owner will provide a chair before the room becomes available, so I will not need to buy one. That is correct. The kitchen is shared by three tenants, including you. There are separate shelves in the refrigerator, although cooking equipment is shared. The current tenants have agreed to label their own food, which has worked better than trying to divide all purchases equally. I am happy to label my food. My main concern is getting to the university early for experiments. The listing says there is a direct bus, but cycling might be more reliable. I noticed a covered bicycle store behind the building, and I would use that regularly. Access to the bicycle store comes with the room key. There is no parking space for a car, however, and the street has a residents-only restriction. This has not caused difficulty for the current tenants because neither owns a car, but I want to make it clear before you decide. I will not have a car, so that is not a problem. I would like to view the room next Thursday. I first suggested the morning in my email, but my train arrives at lunchtime. An appointment at half past two would leave enough time to reach your office. Half past two is available. Meet our representative at the bakery on the corner, because the main entrance is difficult to find from the street. She will carry a folder with the office name on it and take you through the side passage to the building. Thank you. I will bring the reference letter you requested from my previous landlord. I understand that you do not need a payment at the viewing. If I decide to take the room, the deposit can be arranged afterwards through the office’s secure payment system.

You asked about the room on Market Street, but someone reserved it this morning. We still have a room on Willow Road, close to the same bus route. Willow Road could work well for me. I am arriving for a six-month research placement, and I would rather share a flat than live alone. I see the available room is on the second floor. That is fine, because I do not have much luggage to carry upstairs. The rent is five hundred and forty pounds per month. That includes water and heating, but electricity is paid separately according to the meter. Internet access is included as well. We explain the separate electricity arrangement in the contract so there should be no surprise after you move in. That arrangement seems reasonable. The photograph shows a desk, which I will need for reading. I do not see a chair beside it, though. According to the written description, the owner will provide a chair before the room becomes available, so I will not need to buy one. That is correct. The kitchen is shared by three tenants, including you. There are separate shelves in the refrigerator, although cooking equipment is shared. The current tenants have agreed to label their own food, which has worked better than trying to divide all purchases equally. I am happy to label my food. My main concern is getting to the university early for experiments. The listing says there is a direct bus, but cycling might be more reliable. I noticed a covered bicycle store behind the building, and I would use that regularly. Access to the bicycle store comes with the room key. There is no parking space for a car, however, and the street has a residents-only restriction. This has not caused difficulty for the current tenants because neither owns a car, but I want to make it clear before you decide. I will not have a car, so that is not a problem. I would like to view the room next Thursday. I first suggested the morning in my email, but my train arrives at lunchtime. An appointment at half past two would leave enough time to reach your office. Half past two is available. Meet our representative at the bakery on the corner, because the main entrance is difficult to find from the street. She will carry a folder with the office name on it and take you through the side passage to the building. Thank you. I will bring the reference letter you requested from my previous landlord. I understand that you do not need a payment at the viewing. If I decide to take the room, the deposit can be arranged afterwards through the office’s secure payment system.

exercises.transcript: Welcome to the Eastbrook allotments. This is a synthetic practice recording introducing a fictional community garden. Each new member receives a numbered plot and access to shared facilities. Your plot number appears on a wooden marker at the nearest corner, so please check it before moving any equipment. The annual membership covers water use and maintenance of the paths. Seeds are not included because members choose what they want to grow. Our noticeboard sometimes advertises seed exchanges, but those are informal arrangements between members rather than a guaranteed part of the membership package. There are two water taps. Use the one beside the shed during your first month, because the tap near the boundary is being replaced. Both locations are marked on the map, but a temporary sign points to the tap that is currently available. Please fill a watering can rather than attaching a hose. This helps members notice how much water they are using and keeps hoses from lying across the narrow paths. Several cans are stored outside the shed, and you should return them there after watering your plot. The large compost bins stand behind the hedge. You may add vegetable peelings and untreated plant material, but please keep cooked food out. We turn the contents on volunteer mornings so that the material breaks down evenly instead of remaining in separate layers throughout the year. If you borrow tools, write your plot number in the notebook inside the shed. This is not a charge for borrowing; it simply helps us locate a tool when someone else needs it. Do not lend shared tools to people working outside the allotment site. Our first shared work morning is on the nineteenth of this month. It was originally planned for the twelfth, but several members are unavailable then. We will clear the entrance path and repair a bench before stopping for tea, so there will be jobs suitable for different abilities. Children are welcome when accompanied by an adult. The shallow pond is fenced, but adults remain responsible for supervising children throughout a visit. Please do not interpret the fence as permission to leave younger visitors alone while you work at the far end of your plot. We ask members to keep the paths clear. A wheelbarrow may be left beside your plot briefly while unloading, but it should not remain there overnight. Emergency access is the main concern; the rule is not simply intended to make photographs of the garden look tidy. Finally, check the noticeboard near the gate before each visit. Urgent messages are also sent by email, but the board contains routine updates and offers from other members. If your contact details change, tell the secretary so important messages do not continue going to an unused address.
