exercises.transcript: Thanks for meeting before class. This is a synthetic practice discussion about our fictional history podcast project. We initially considered famous buildings, but the tutor suggested a narrower focus. I think the old railway station gives us enough material for a short episode without covering the whole town. I agree with that choice. The assignment asks for an episode lasting twelve minutes, including the introduction and credits. We should not plan twelve minutes of interviews and then add everything else, because the tutor said the complete recording must stay within the same limit. For background information, I have found a collection of local newspapers in the library. A few websites repeat the same story without identifying where it came from. The newspapers should help us distinguish contemporary reports from details that were added much later in popular accounts. That will be useful, but we should still include a personal perspective. My neighbour worked at the station as a porter, and he is willing to speak with us. His memories will not establish every historical fact, so we should compare dates he mentions with your written sources. Before recording him, we need written permission. The tutor gave us a consent form that explains where the audio may be shared and allows the speaker to decline particular questions. I will print it and give him time to read it before the interview begins. For the interview location, I first thought of the station café because it would sound atmospheric. On reflection, the noise would make his voice difficult to understand. His sitting room is quieter, and we can add a brief separate recording of station sounds later. That is sensible. I can borrow a microphone from the media office, but we should test it before the interview rather than assuming it works. I will also make a short practice recording so we can find a comfortable distance between the microphone and the speaker. While you arrange the equipment, I will prepare the questions. I want to begin with daily routines rather than ask for opinions immediately. Describing an ordinary working day may help our neighbour remember concrete details before we move on to how the station changed over time. After we have selected the interview extracts, we can write the narration around them. I do not want to write a complete script first and force his answers into it. The strongest extracts should determine which points need explanation and where listeners need help following the chronology. Let us send a rough edit to the tutor on Friday. The final deadline is Monday, but an earlier version leaves time to act on comments. We should label it clearly as a draft so the tutor knows that the sound levels and final credits may still change.

exercises.transcript: This is a synthetic practice lecture about a fictional student research project. The team investigated why customers left food on their plates in a campus canteen. Their aim was to understand waste after purchase, so they did not measure ingredients discarded in the kitchen before meals were served. The students observed the canteen for five weekdays. They deliberately avoided a festival week because special menus and visiting groups might have made the results less typical. Their report acknowledges that one ordinary week still cannot represent every season or every type of campus event. At the collection station, customers placed their plates on a tray. The students first removed bones and other inedible material, then weighed the remaining food. This separation mattered because a heavy collection of bones would otherwise appear to be a large amount of food that someone could have eaten. The team also offered a short questionnaire. They asked customers to select their main reason for leaving food, rather than write a long account. This made participation quick, but it meant the researchers had to decide on useful answer categories before they knew every possible explanation. In the invented results used for this exercise, large portions were the most frequently selected reason. Poor flavour was mentioned less often than the researchers had expected. They therefore changed the emphasis of their presentation instead of keeping an argument that their own observations did not support. There was an important limitation: people who returned an empty plate could still decline the questionnaire. The respondents might therefore differ from those who did not respond. We should not assume that offering every customer a form automatically produces a representative set of completed responses. To improve their measurement procedure, the students tested the scales using a standard weight each morning. This check could reveal a change in the instrument, but it could not correct a poorly chosen questionnaire category. Different parts of a research design need different kinds of quality checks. The report compared waste from meals with different portion options. However, customers chose their own meals, so the comparison did not randomly assign portion size. Someone selecting a larger meal might also differ in appetite or available lunch time, which complicates a simple causal explanation. For a future pilot, the team proposed offering a smaller default serving while allowing customers to request more. They recommended testing that change before introducing it permanently. Their proposal aimed to preserve choice, rather than forcing everyone to accept the same quantity regardless of appetite. The final presentation will include a chart of the reported reasons and a separate table of measured weights. Keeping these forms of evidence distinct is essential. A questionnaire records what people say, while the scales record a physical quantity; neither should be silently substituted for the other.

Using the same material helped avoid a comparison in which differences in colour or composition might be confused with the effect of shade. Measurements were taken at noon on each observation day. A convenient schedule is useful only if it still allows the comparison the investigation is designed to make. Before collecting data, the students marked the measurement points with small pieces of tape. Returning to those positions reduced variation caused by measuring a different patch of wall each day. The tape was placed beside each point so the instrument still measured the brick itself. The teacher reminded everyone to record the cloud cover as well. A cloudy day might reduce the difference between shaded and exposed sections. Recording that condition would not remove its effect, but it would help readers understand why results might differ across observation days. In the fictional data, the shaded section was cooler on most days. On one heavily overcast day the readings were almost equal. The students kept that result in their report instead of deleting it simply because it was less consistent with the pattern they expected to find. When presenting the findings, the group used a line graph to show changes across days. Each section of wall had its own line. Clear labels were more useful than decorative effects, because readers needed to follow the same section consistently from the first observation to the last. The screen was removed after the observation period so the class could discuss reversibility. The teacher did not claim the temporary screen was the best permanent solution for every building. Maintenance, wind exposure, and access requirements would also matter when considering a real installation outside this classroom example. For a follow-up study, students suggested repeating the observations in winter. That would help them explore whether the same shading arrangement has different consequences in another season. They would keep the measurement positions and timing comparable, while clearly describing any changes in the procedure. Finally, the report separates observations from interpretations. The instrument readings belong in the results section. Possible explanations, including the role of cloud cover, belong in the discussion. Readers can then see what was measured directly and what the class inferred from those measurements.

exercises.transcript: Welcome to this training session for our fictional local museum. This is a synthetic practice recording. Today you will catalogue donated household objects, beginning with the wooden box on each table. Leave fragile glass objects for trained staff until you have completed the introductory handling session. Every object receives an identification number before anyone writes a description. Please copy that number from the label into the top field of the form. Do not create a new number because the existing label looks untidy; the old number connects the object with earlier records. Record the main material next. If an object combines wood and metal, list both instead of deciding that the smaller component is unimportant. Where you are uncertain, write unknown and ask the supervisor. Guessing may make the record look complete while reducing its reliability for future users. For dimensions, use millimetres throughout the form. Another department uses centimetres, but mixing units within our catalogue would create errors. Measure the greatest length, width, and height, and note separately if an irregular shape makes one of those measurements difficult to define. exercises.transcript: Thank you for helping with our fictional charity walk. This is a synthetic practice recording for route volunteers. The event raises funds for a community kitchen, and participants will follow a marked route through the town. Your role is to guide walkers, not to collect donations along the path. Collect your volunteer pack from the school gym between eight and half past eight. Registration was originally planned for the playground, but rain is forecast. The gym entrance is on the side street, and a member of staff will direct you there from the main gate. Each pack contains a route map and an emergency contact card. Keep the card with you throughout the event rather than leaving it in your bag at registration. The number on it reaches the event control team, which can coordinate a response across the whole route. The first walkers leave at nine. Volunteers need to reach their positions twenty minutes earlier, so please leave the gym promptly after collecting your pack. We will not delay the whole event because someone stops for breakfast on the way to their assigned point. At junctions, point to the direction shown on your map. Do not create a shortcut even if it seems easier, because the control team needs to know where participants are travelling. The planned route also avoids a road where repairs have narrowed the pavement this week. The water station is beside the library. Last year it stood at the fountain, but that area is now occupied by maintenance equipment. Tell walkers about the library station before they reach the turning, particularly if they are looking for the location they remember from last year. If a walker wishes to stop, contact event control and remain with the person until further instructions arrive. Volunteers should not offer transport in their own cars. The event has an arranged collection procedure so that the team can account for everyone who leaves the route early. Please record the approximate number of walkers passing your position at fifteen-minute intervals. We do not need names at each junction. These counts help us see how the group is spreading out and decide whether a later station is likely to need additional supplies. A cyclist wearing an orange vest will follow the final walker. Remain at your position until that cyclist passes, even if the route has looked empty for several minutes. A gap in the group does not prove that everyone has already gone through your junction. After the cyclist passes, return the route signs to the school gym. You may keep the printed map, but the signs will be used again. Hand your count sheet to the coordinator before leaving so the information is available when the team reviews the event tomorrow.

exercises.transcript: This is a synthetic practice lecture about an invented field investigation. A class studied small rock pools on a sheltered shore, asking how conditions differed between pools at different heights. The exercise was about comparing habitats, not collecting animals to take back to the classroom. The teacher divided the shore into three zones. These zones were based on height above the water at low tide rather than on distance from the nearest car park. Each group worked in one zone so the class could combine observations without repeatedly visiting the same pools. Within a zone, students selected pools using numbered locations on a prepared grid. Choosing only the largest or most attractive pools would have biased the comparison. The grid did not guarantee a perfect sample, but it provided a method that another class could understand and repeat. The first measurement was water depth at the centre of each pool. Students used the same marked ruler and recorded the result in centimetres. They avoided pressing the ruler into soft sediment because that would measure part of the bottom as though it were water. Next, the groups recorded the number of visible snails without moving rocks. The teacher emphasised that this was a count of animals they could see, not necessarily every animal present. Hidden organisms remained outside the observation, so the wording of the result needed to preserve that limitation. Some students wanted to record every species they encountered. For this short exercise, the teacher restricted the task to one recognisable group. A narrower question could be answered consistently within the available time, whereas an incomplete list of many unfamiliar species might be difficult to compare. Clouds moved across the sun during the morning, and students recorded the time of each visit. This helped the class discuss whether pools measured later had experienced different conditions. The teacher did not allow students to treat all readings as simultaneous simply because they were collected on the same day. In the fictional results, higher pools showed a wider range of water depths than lower pools. That observation did not establish that height alone caused the difference. Pool shape and recent wave action could also matter, so the discussion considered several plausible influences rather than announcing one certain cause. For the follow-up, students proposed revisiting the same pools after a week. Matching the locations would help distinguish change within a pool from differences between newly selected pools. They would still record weather and timing, because revisiting a location does not hold every environmental condition constant. Before leaving, the class checked that no equipment remained on the shore. Animals and rocks were left where they had been found. The final report included a method diagram so readers could see the zones and selection grid without mistaking the drawing for a precise map of every pool.

exercises.author: StylishSAT original AI-authored expansion, 2026-09-05; synthetic eSpeak NG audio; independent IELTS specialist and listening review pending
exercises.transcript: This is a synthetic practice discussion between two students preparing a fictional facilities proposal. Our tutor asked us to choose one change that could improve an existing study room. I first thought about extending opening hours, but we do not have enough information about staffing costs to evaluate that properly. Then let us focus on noise within the room. Students use the same area for silent reading and group discussion, which creates competing expectations. We could propose dividing the room into zones without claiming that conversation is always inappropriate in a university study space. Before suggesting a layout, we should observe how the room is currently used. I propose three visits at different times of day rather than one long visit on a quiet morning. That should show whether the pattern changes when students arrive between lectures or stay into the evening. We should count occupied seats and note the locations of conversations. We do not need to record people’s names or what they say. The purpose is to understand activity patterns, and collecting personal details would add information that is unnecessary for the layout question we are trying to answer. For a rough plan, the silent zone could be beside the windows. There are already individual desks there, and the daylight is useful for reading. I would leave the larger tables near the entrance for conversation so groups do not walk through the quiet section whenever someone joins them. That could work, but a sign alone may not change behaviour. We should ask students whether movable screens would make the boundary clearer. The screens would not soundproof the room, and our proposal should avoid suggesting that a lightweight divider can completely block normal conversation. I can prepare a short survey with a sketch of both zones. We should include an option for people who prefer the current arrangement, rather than offering only different versions of our proposal. Otherwise, the form would push respondents towards agreeing that some change is necessary. After the survey, we could suggest a trial lasting two weeks. Permanent furniture changes would be premature before seeing how the zones work in practice. During the trial, the staff could keep a simple record of complaints and compare it with observations from the earlier period. We need to be careful with that comparison. Fewer complaints would not necessarily mean less noise; students might simply be busy elsewhere. We should look at occupancy as well, so any claim about improvement considers how many people actually used the room during each observation period. Let us divide the work now. You will draw the plan, and I will draft the survey. We can meet on Tuesday to combine them, even though the proposal is not due until Thursday. Meeting earlier gives us a chance to remove unclear wording before submission.

exercises.author: StylishSAT original AI-authored expansion, 2026-09-05; synthetic eSpeak NG audio; independent IELTS specialist and listening review pending
exercises.transcript: This is a synthetic practice discussion between two students preparing a fictional facilities proposal. Our tutor asked us to choose one change that could improve an existing study room. I first thought about extending opening hours, but we do not have enough information about staffing costs to evaluate that properly. Then let us focus on noise within the room. Students use the same area for silent reading and group discussion, which creates competing expectations. We could propose dividing the room into zones without claiming that conversation is always inappropriate in a university study space. Before suggesting a layout, we should observe how the room is currently used. I propose three visits at different times of day rather than one long visit on a quiet morning. That should show whether the pattern changes when students arrive between lectures or stay into the evening. We should count occupied seats and note the locations of conversations. We do not need to record people’s names or what they say. The purpose is to understand activity patterns, and collecting personal details would add information that is unnecessary for the layout question we are trying to answer. For a rough plan, the silent zone could be beside the windows. There are already individual desks there, and the daylight is useful for reading. I would leave the larger tables near the entrance for conversation so groups do not walk through the quiet section whenever someone joins them. That could work, but a sign alone may not change behaviour. We should ask students whether movable screens would make the boundary clearer. The screens would not soundproof the room, and our proposal should avoid suggesting that a lightweight divider can completely block normal conversation. I can prepare a short survey with a sketch of both zones. We should include an option for people who prefer the current arrangement, rather than offering only different versions of our proposal. Otherwise, the form would push respondents towards agreeing that some change is necessary. After the survey, we could suggest a trial lasting two weeks. Permanent furniture changes would be premature before seeing how the zones work in practice. During the trial, the staff could keep a simple record of complaints and compare it with observations from the earlier period. We need to be careful with that comparison. Fewer complaints would not necessarily mean less noise; students might simply be busy elsewhere. We should look at occupancy as well, so any claim about improvement considers how many people actually used the room during each observation period. Let us divide the work now. You will draw the plan, and I will draft the survey. We can meet on Tuesday to combine them, even though the proposal is not due until Thursday. Meeting earlier gives us a chance to remove unclear wording before submission.

exercises.transcript: Hello, community music office. This is a synthetic practice conversation about a fictional instrument loan. You asked whether your daughter could borrow a violin, and one is now available. We will need her teacher to confirm the correct size before we complete the loan agreement. That is helpful. Her teacher has already recommended a three-quarter size instrument. She has tried a full-size one, but it was uncomfortable. I can bring the teacher’s note to the office, so you do not have to rely only on what I remember from the lesson. Please bring the note. The loan fee is eighteen pounds per month, and the case is included. A refundable deposit is separate from that monthly amount. We will list both clearly on the agreement so that you can distinguish the continuing charge from money held until the instrument is returned. I understand the difference. My main question is whether the bow is included, because the teacher said a suitable bow matters as much as the instrument. I do not want to purchase one and then discover that the loan package already provides everything she needs for her first lessons. Yes, a bow is included. Rosin is included too, but your daughter will need her own shoulder rest, fitted with the teacher’s help. Different players find different supports comfortable, so we leave that choice to the teacher rather than supplying one model to every borrower. That makes sense. We would like to collect the instrument on Saturday if possible. I originally wrote Friday on the application, but her teacher can join us only the following day. Having the teacher there would allow us to check the fit before taking the instrument home. Saturday morning is fine. Come to the rehearsal room behind the main office. We use that space for collections so borrowers can try an instrument without disturbing staff on the telephone. The main office remains the place to return completed paperwork after you have finished checking the fit. We will do that. I have also read the care instructions about keeping the violin away from heaters. Our daughter’s room can get warm in the afternoon, so we will store the case in the hallway instead of beside her bedroom window or the radiator. Please contact us before arranging any repair. Our appointed technician handles work on loan instruments, and the agreement does not permit borrowers to use another repairer without approval. That protects the instrument’s record and ensures we know about changes before lending it to the next player. Thank you. We will keep the contact card inside the case. I see that the first review is after six months, when you will ask whether the size is still suitable. That seems sensible because she may grow before the full year of lessons has finished.

exercises.transcript: This is a synthetic practice lecture about an invented study of clothing donations. The researchers followed garments through a local sorting centre to examine what happened after donation. They focused on reuse as clothing, which is different from turning fabric into industrial wiping cloths or other recycled products. The centre received donations from collection bins and from a staffed counter. The team recorded the two sources separately because items handed to a member of staff might differ from bags left anonymously. Combining both streams immediately would hide a distinction that could help interpret the sorting results. Each sampled garment received a temporary code. This allowed the team to follow it between sorting stages without writing a donor’s name on the record. The code tracked the garment, not its original buyer or wearer. Sorters first checked whether an item was dry. Wet garments were set aside because moisture could affect other items stored nearby. The researchers recorded this initial condition separately from later decisions about style, size, or visible damage, since those decisions answered different questions about possible reuse. The next stage considered repairs. A missing button was treated differently from a large tear across the fabric. Staff estimated the work needed before deciding whether a repair was practical within the centre’s resources. The study did not assume that every technically possible repair would be economical to perform. In the fictional sample, labels were often too faded to read. The team therefore reported material information as unknown when it could not be established reliably. They did not guess fabric composition from appearance alone, because a confident-looking guess could distort comparisons between different material categories. The researchers visited on four separate days. They chose days across the month rather than four consecutive mornings, hoping to capture some variation in incoming donations. That choice broadened the observation window, but the report still described the sample as limited to one centre and one month. One chart showed the proportion of garments reaching each sorting stage. Another showed the staff time used for repairs. These charts measured different things. A category containing relatively few garments could still require substantial work, so the researchers avoided equating item counts with labour requirements. The report noted that sorting decisions can change with local demand. A garment accepted during one season might be less useful during another. Consequently, the invented study does not support a universal list of items that every centre should accept regardless of storage space, customers, or time of year. For a follow-up, the researchers proposed repeating the same tracking procedure at another centre. Using compatible categories would make comparison easier, while recording local differences would prevent misleading conclusions. Repeating the method would be valuable precisely because the second centre might not produce the same pattern as the first.

exercises.transcript: This is a synthetic practice discussion about a fictional archive project. We need to interview a former resident of the riverside housing estate. The archive already has maps and building plans, but it lacks accounts of everyday life, so that should be the focus of our conversation. I have contacted a woman who lived there for twenty years. She is willing to take part but would prefer a short first meeting before we switch on the recorder. That seems reasonable, because she wants to understand the project rather than arrive expecting an ordinary social visit. At the first meeting, we should explain that she may decline any question. We must also ask separately whether the recording can be made publicly accessible. Agreeing to speak with us is not automatically the same as agreeing that unknown listeners may hear the recording in the future. For prompts, I could bring a photograph of the estate’s courtyard. A picture may help her recall where people gathered, without requiring us to suggest a particular answer. We should avoid treating her response as incorrect simply because it differs from the caption written on the archive’s copy. Let us start with open questions about a typical day. A question such as whether everyone was friendly would push towards a general judgement too soon. Asking what she did after returning from work should make space for concrete events and for experiences we have not anticipated. We also need to decide how to handle dates. If she is uncertain, we can record an approximate period rather than press her to choose an exact year. Later, we may compare that recollection with other sources, while keeping clear which part comes from memory and which from a document. I will take responsibility for monitoring the recorder. That does not mean interrupting every time someone pauses. Silence can give an interviewee time to remember, and filling it immediately with another question may cut off an account just as the speaker is deciding how to continue. Afterwards, we should produce a transcript and send it to her for checking. She may correct a name that we heard wrongly or point out a section she does not want shared. We need to keep a record of agreed changes instead of silently rewriting the account into our own preferred wording. For the archive description, we should include the interview date and location, along with the agreed access conditions. Those details help future users understand the source. A polished summary alone would not explain where the account came from or whether all of it may be quoted publicly. Our next step is to confirm the introductory meeting for Wednesday. The actual recorded interview can be arranged afterwards; it is not fixed for that day. I will write a clear message so she does not think she needs to prepare a complete account before our first short conversation.

I have contacted a woman who lived there for twenty years. She is willing to take part but would prefer a short first meeting before we switch on the recorder. That seems reasonable, because she wants to understand the project rather than arrive expecting an ordinary social visit.

At the first meeting, we should explain that she may decline any question. We must also ask separately whether the recording can be made publicly accessible. Agreeing to speak with us is not automatically the same as agreeing that unknown listeners may hear the recording in the future.

For prompts, I could bring a photograph of the estate’s courtyard. A picture may help her recall where people gathered, without requiring us to suggest a particular answer. We should avoid treating her response as incorrect simply because it differs from the caption written on the archive’s copy.

Let us start with open questions about a typical day. A question such as whether everyone was friendly would push towards a general judgement too soon. Asking what she did after returning from work should make space for concrete events and for experiences we have not anticipated.

We also need to decide how to handle dates. If she is uncertain, we can record an approximate period rather than press her to choose an exact year. Later, we may compare that recollection with other sources, while keeping clear which part comes from memory and which from a document.

I will take responsibility for monitoring the recorder. That does not mean interrupting every time someone pauses. Silence can give an interviewee time to remember, and filling it immediately with another question may cut off an account just as the speaker is deciding how to continue.

Afterwards, we should produce a transcript and send it to her for checking. She may correct a name that we heard wrongly or point out a section she does not want shared. We need to keep a record of agreed changes instead of silently rewriting the account into our own preferred wording.

For the archive description, we should include the interview date and location, along with the agreed access conditions. Those details help future users understand the source. A polished summary alone would not explain where the account came from or whether all of it may be quoted publicly.

Our next step is to confirm the introductory meeting for Wednesday. The actual recorded interview can be arranged afterwards; it is not fixed for that day. I will write a clear message so she does not think she needs to prepare a complete account before our first short conversation.

You asked for a programme about the Moon, but that presentation is unavailable during your visit week. We can offer the programme about navigation, which connects the night sky with finding directions. Navigation would fit our geography work well. We will bring twenty-six pupils rather than the thirty I first estimated. Four are attending a sports event that day. There will also be three adults, but I understand that you need the pupil and adult counts recorded separately on the booking. Thank you for separating those numbers. Your group’s presentation begins at eleven forty-five. We recommend arriving half an hour beforehand because pupils need time to use the toilets and put away bags. That arrival allowance is separate from the presentation’s advertised starting time. We can arrive early. Our coach driver asked where to stop because the front entrance faces a narrow road. The instructions you sent mention the service entrance on Park Lane. I will send those directions to the driver so we do not block the road while the pupils get out. That is the correct entrance. A member of staff will meet you there and lead the class to the lockers. Please leave large bags in those lockers before entering the dome, because the seating aisles must remain clear throughout the presentation, including while the lights are dimmed. I will remind the pupils. One child is sensitive to sudden loud sounds, so I am interested in the accessibility notes. They say the session has a spoken introduction before the lights change. That should help the class understand what is about to happen rather than being surprised by the darkened room. The presenter can also explain the sound levels before the programme. After the dome session, your group has a practical activity using compasses. These are supplied by us, so pupils do not need to bring their own equipment. The activity is designed to connect the presentation with simple observations outdoors. That will be useful. We plan to bring packed lunches because the café would take too long for a group this size. I see that the covered terrace is available for school groups. We will use that space and make sure everyone takes their rubbish back to the collection point afterwards. Please confirm the final numbers by the Monday before your visit. We used to request confirmation on Friday, but that left too little time to prepare the activity materials. You can update the booking online, and the system will send a new confirmation showing any changes. I will update the booking by then. Please send the invoice to our school office rather than to my personal email. The office handles payments and needs the reference number on its own copy. I will still keep the visit confirmation for the teaching arrangements and arrival instructions.

exercises.author: StylishSAT original AI-authored expansion, 2026-09-05; synthetic eSpeak NG audio; independent IELTS specialist and listening review pending
exercises.transcript: This is a synthetic practice lecture about a fictional environmental recording project. Students investigated how a stream’s sound changed at different points along its course. Their question concerned the recorded sound, not whether one location was more pleasant for visitors, which would require evidence about people’s responses. The team selected six recording points between a small bridge and a footpath crossing. Each point received a number on a sketch map. The map showed enough detail for a return visit without claiming to be an accurate survey of the entire valley or the stream’s full length. At every point, the microphone was held at the same height above the water. Students used a marked pole to check that position. They also kept the recorder’s input setting unchanged, because automatic changes in recording level could make two similar sounds appear different in the resulting files. Each recording lasted forty seconds. The students waited quietly before pressing the record button so footsteps and conversation would not dominate the opening. A longer file would not automatically be better if it contained more movement by the people collecting it instead of the stream they wanted to study. The field notes included recent rainfall as reported by a nearby weather station. This did not tell the students exactly how much water passed each recording point. It did, however, provide context for discussing why recordings made on different days might not be directly comparable without further measurements. One recording contained a passing motorcycle. The team labelled that interval instead of pretending it was part of the water sound. They retained the original file and documented any section excluded from the analysis, allowing another listener to understand how the processed sample differed from the original recording. In the fictional analysis, recordings near small drops contained more rapid fluctuations than recordings beside a smooth stretch. The lecturer cautioned that this comparison alone could not isolate the effect of the drops. Water volume, nearby surfaces, and microphone surroundings might also influence the recorded pattern. For visual comparison, the students displayed waveforms on a shared time scale. They resisted stretching each file differently just to fill the available page width. Consistent display settings mattered because a reader might otherwise attribute a visual difference to the sound when it actually came from how the figure was drawn. A follow-up proposal involved recording the same points after a dry period. The team would keep the microphone position and recording settings comparable. The comparison would still need careful field notes, because repeating equipment settings does not make every feature of an outdoor environment remain unchanged. The final report kept the original recordings alongside a description of the analysis procedure. A short audio excerpt could illustrate a point in the presentation, but it could not replace the complete evidence. Readers needed to know how the excerpt was selected before judging how well it represented the wider set.

exercises.author: StylishSAT original AI-authored expansion, 2026-09-05; synthetic eSpeak NG audio; independent IELTS specialist and listening review pending
exercises.transcript: This is a synthetic practice lecture describing a fictional classroom demonstration of seed storage. The class compared batches of the same seed variety under different conditions. The aim was to design a careful comparison, not to recommend a storage method for every crop or to report a real agricultural trial. The teacher divided the seeds into labelled paper envelopes. Each envelope held thirty seeds, so later counts could be compared using the same starting total. Students wrote the batch code before filling the envelope, reducing the chance of confusing two groups when several people worked at the table. One set was stored in a cool cupboard and another in a warmer room. Both remained away from direct sunlight. The class recorded the actual temperature rather than relying only on the words cool and warm, since those labels would be too vague for someone trying to repeat the demonstration. The envelopes were inspected once a week without opening every packet. Students checked the labels and looked for signs that the storage area had become damp. If a packet was moved, the change was written in the log rather than remembered informally until the final presentation several weeks later. After the storage period, seeds from each batch were placed on moist paper for a germination check. The amount of water was kept consistent across dishes. Otherwise, a difference during this later check could be mistaken for an effect of the earlier storage condition the class actually wanted to compare. The class agreed on a visible criterion before counting a seed as germinated: a root had to emerge. They did not change the rule after seeing the results. A clear criterion made it easier for different students to classify the same seed consistently instead of relying on a general impression. In the fictional results, one batch had fewer germinated seeds at the first count but caught up later. The teacher therefore asked students to distinguish the speed of germination from the eventual proportion germinated. Reporting only the earliest count would have hidden that difference between two possible outcomes. A few seeds showed signs of mould during the check. The class recorded those observations separately instead of silently removing the seeds from the denominator. Changing the starting total after seeing an inconvenient outcome would make the reported proportions difficult for readers to interpret or reproduce. The teacher reminded students that a small classroom batch has limited scope. They had not tested many varieties or repeated the demonstration across several years. The report could describe what happened in this example while explaining why broader recommendations would require substantially more evidence. For the final display, students showed both the raw counts and the calculated percentages. This allowed visitors to see the small number of seeds behind each percentage. They also displayed the written procedure, so the visual presentation communicated how the observations were obtained rather than presenting numbers without context.

Students wrote the batch code before filling the envelope, reducing the chance of confusing two groups when several people worked at the table.

One set was stored in a cool cupboard and another in a warmer room. Both remained away from direct sunlight. The class recorded the actual temperature rather than relying only on the words cool and warm, since those labels would be too vague for someone trying to repeat the demonstration.

The envelopes were inspected once a week without opening every packet. Students checked the labels and looked for signs that the storage area had become damp. If a packet was moved, the change was written in the log rather than remembered informally until the final presentation several weeks later.

After the storage period, seeds from each batch were placed on moist paper for a germination check. The amount of water was kept consistent across dishes. Otherwise, a difference during this later check could be mistaken for an effect of the earlier storage condition the class actually wanted to compare.

The class agreed on a visible criterion before counting a seed as germinated: a root had to emerge. They did not change the rule after seeing the results. A clear criterion made it easier for different students to classify the same seed consistently instead of relying on a general impression.

In the fictional results, one batch had fewer germinated seeds at the first count but caught up later. The teacher therefore asked students to distinguish the speed of germination from the eventual proportion germinated. Reporting only the earliest count would have hidden that difference between two possible outcomes.

A few seeds showed signs of mould during the check. The class recorded those observations separately instead of silently removing the seeds from the denominator. Changing the starting total after seeing an inconvenient outcome would make the reported proportions difficult for readers to interpret or reproduce.

The teacher reminded students that a small classroom batch has limited scope. They had not tested many varieties or repeated the demonstration across several years. The report could describe what happened in this example while explaining why broader recommendations would require substantially more evidence.

For the final display, students showed both the raw counts and the calculated percentages. This allowed visitors to see the small number of seeds behind each percentage. They also displayed the written procedure, so the visual presentation communicated how the observations were obtained rather than presenting numbers without context.

exercises.prompt: Short Academic Task 1 diagnostic: The chart shows the shares of three fruit categories in total fruit sales at fictional Noma Market in 2018 and 2024. Summarise the main features and make relevant comparisons. Write at least 90 words in about 6 minutes. This is an abbreviated skill probe; a full Task 1 response requires at least 150 words. All figures are fictional percentages of the mass of fruit sold, not percentages of customers.

explanation.en:
Task achievement: State that plums replaced apples as the largest category. Support this with 25% to 45% for plums and 40% to 25% for apples; pears declined slightly.

Coherence and cohesion: Separate an overview of changing rank from the supporting figures. Group the two declining categories instead of making six disconnected statements.

Lexical resource: Use share, accounted for and percentage points accurately. The plum increase is 20 percentage points; total sales mass is not provided.

Grammatical range and accuracy: Use past tense for both years, and check agreement in phrases such as the share of apples fell.

This is formative practice guidance; no official band is assigned.
explanation.ru:
Выполнение задания: Укажите, что сливы сменили яблоки как крупнейшую категорию. Подтвердите 25%→45% для слив и 40%→25% для яблок; груши немного снизились.

Связность и организация: Отделите обзор смены лидера от чисел. Объедините две снижающиеся категории вместо шести разрозненных утверждений.

Лексика: Точно используйте share, accounted for и percentage points. Рост слив — 20 процентных пунктов; общая масса продаж не дана.

Грамматический диапазон и точность: Используйте прошедшее время для обоих лет и согласование в the share of apples fell.

Это тренировочные рекомендации; официальный band не выставляется.

hints.ru: До записи чисел определите лидирующую категорию каждого года.

hints.en: Compare the largest rise with the largest fall and label changes in percentage points.
hints.ru: Сопоставьте наибольший рост с наибольшим падением и обозначьте изменения в процентных пунктах.

typicalErrors.ru: Принятие долей массы фруктов за доли покупателей.

typicalErrors.ru: Обозначение роста 25%→45% как 20 процентов без различения процентных пунктов.

typicalErrors.en: Inventing prices, preferences or reasons for the changes.

exercises.prompt: Academic Task 1: The chart compares annual admissions to indoor and outdoor pools operated by fictional Bellis Leisure in 2018, 2020, 2022 and 2024. Summarise the main features and make relevant comparisons. Write at least 150 words in about 20 minutes. All values are fictional and measured in thousands of admissions; one person may make several admissions.

explanation.en:
Illustrative AI-authored sample; no band assigned.

Task achievement: “rose initially, then declined” accurately summarises the outdoor direction change, and “a net increase of only 5 thousand” distinguishes the overall result from the decline after 2020. Refinement: the initial two-to-one indoor/outdoor ratio could provide another concise comparison.

Coherence and cohesion: “Indoor pools recorded” and “Outdoor admissions started” mark the two detail groups clearly. Refinement: connect the final whole-period comparison more directly to the overview rather than relying on a separate closing summary.

Lexical resource: “admissions” preserves the unit, and “a peak of 45 thousand” accurately labels the maximum. Refinement: replace a repeated “increased” with “rose” only where the change and figure remain exact; avoid forced synonyms for admissions.

Grammatical range and accuracy: “although it finished above its starting level” gives a correct concessive clause. Refinement: a while-clause could combine the final two net changes without changing their meaning. These are editing options, not invented errors.
explanation.ru:
Иллюстративный ИИ-образец; band не выставляется.

Выполнение задания: «rose initially, then declined» точно обобщает смену направления открытых бассейнов, а «a net increase of only 5 thousand» отличает итог от снижения после 2020. Уточнение: исходное отношение крытых к открытым два к одному могло бы дать ещё одно краткое сравнение.

Связность: «Indoor pools recorded» и «Outdoor admissions started» ясно отмечают две группы деталей. Уточнение: свяжите итоговое сравнение за период непосредственно с обзором, не полагаясь на отдельное заключительное обобщение.

Лексика: «admissions» сохраняет единицу, «a peak of 45 thousand» точно обозначает максимум. Уточнение: заменяйте повтор increased на rose только с сохранением точного смысла; избегайте искусственных синонимов для admissions.

Грамматика: «although it finished above its starting level» даёт верное уступительное придаточное. Уточнение: придаточное с while могло бы объединить два итоговых изменения без смены смысла. Это варианты редактирования, а не выдуманные ошибки.

hints.en: Find whether each series rises throughout or changes direction.
hints.ru: Определите, растёт ли каждый ряд непрерывно или меняет направление.

hints.en: Use 2018, the outdoor peak in 2020 and 2024 to organise comparisons.
hints.ru: Используйте 2018, пик открытых в 2020 и 2024 для организации сравнений.

typicalErrors.ru: Описание посещений как уникальных посетителей.

typicalErrors.en: Saying outdoor admissions fell over the entire period despite 30 rising to 35.
typicalErrors.ru: Заявление о снижении открытых за весь период при росте 30→35.

typicalErrors.en: Attributing the pattern to weather or closures absent from the chart.
typicalErrors.ru: Объяснение динамики погодой или закрытиями, которых нет на графике.

criteria.ru: Связность и организация: Сгруппируйте рост крытых в одном абзаце, рост и падение открытых — в другом, затем прямо сравните конечный разрыв.

chart.title: Pool admissions at fictional Bellis Leisure

exercises.sampleAnswer:
The chart compares annual admissions to indoor and outdoor pools run by Bellis Leisure at four points between 2018 and 2024. Figures are given in thousands of admissions. Overall, indoor admissions increased throughout the period and remained higher than outdoor admissions. The outdoor figure rose initially, then declined, although it finished above its starting level.

Indoor pools recorded 60 thousand admissions in 2018. This increased to 65 thousand in 2020 and 70 thousand in 2022, before reaching 90 thousand in 2024. The final two-year increase, at 20 thousand, was larger than either of the earlier increases.

Outdoor admissions started at 30 thousand and climbed to a peak of 45 thousand in 2020. They then fell to 40 thousand in 2022 and 35 thousand in the final year. Consequently, the gap between the two categories narrowed from 30 thousand in 2018 to 20 thousand in 2020, before widening to 55 thousand by 2024.

Across the whole period, indoor admissions rose by 30 thousand, compared with a net increase of only 5 thousand outdoors. These are admission counts rather than numbers of different swimmers, so repeated visits may contribute to either series.

exercises.prompt: Academic Task 1: The chart shows the proportion of adults in each age group who attended at least one workplace training course in fictional Ester County in 2018 and 2024. Summarise the main features and make relevant comparisons. Write at least 150 words in about 20 minutes. All values are fictional. Each percentage uses that age group as its denominator; the groups need not contain equal numbers of people.

explanation.en:
Task achievement: Identify the youngest group as highest in both years and the oldest as lowest, while noting that the age gap narrowed. Participation rose in every group except ages 20–29.

Coherence and cohesion: Organise by direction of change or compare the two age profiles. Do not add unrelated explanations about employer behaviour.

Lexical resource: Distinguish participation rate from participant count. The oldest group gained 20 percentage points, which is not a claim about twenty additional people.

Grammatical range and accuracy: Compare parallel groups with higher than and lower than; use the group aged 50–59 when a singular verb follows.

This is formative practice guidance; no official band is assigned.
explanation.ru:
Выполнение задания: Назовите младшую группу самой высокой в оба года, старшую — самой низкой, отметив сокращение возрастного разрыва. Участие выросло во всех группах, кроме 20–29.

Связность и организация: Организуйте по направлению изменения либо сопоставьте два возрастных профиля. Не добавляйте неподтверждённые объяснения поведения работодателей.

Лексика: Отличайте долю участия от числа участников. Старшая группа прибавила 20 процентных пунктов, а не двадцать человек.

Грамматический диапазон и точность: Сопоставляйте группы через higher than и lower than; используйте the group aged 50–59 перед глаголом единственного числа.

Это тренировочные рекомендации; официальный band не выставляется.

hints.en: Compare the youngest–oldest gap in each year.
hints.ru: Сравните разрыв младшей и старшей групп в каждом году.

hints.en: Separate the one decline from the three increases; use percentage-point changes.
hints.ru: Отделите единственное падение от трёх увеличений; используйте процентные пункты.

typicalErrors.en: Adding the age-group percentages as though they were shares of one total.
typicalErrors.ru: Сложение процентов возрастных групп как долей одного целого.

typicalErrors.en: Inferring participant totals without group population sizes.

exercises.prompt: Academic Task 1: The chart shows how household waste collected in fictional Marden Borough was treated in 2014, 2019 and 2024. Summarise the main features and make relevant comparisons. Write at least 150 words in about 20 minutes. All figures are fictional percentages of collected waste mass. Recycling, landfill and composting are the only treatment categories in this dataset.

explanation.en:
Illustrative AI-authored sample; no band assigned.

Task achievement: “lost its dominant position as recycling expanded” identifies the principal change; “25% each” correctly describes the final equality. Refinement: explicitly compare recycling’s 2024 share with its 2014 level as two and a half times as large if a ratio adds value.

Coherence and cohesion: “Five years later” and “By 2024” guide a chronological structure, while the overview keeps the whole pattern visible. Refinement: the final limitation could be integrated into the detail paragraph to reduce an extra closing paragraph.

Lexical resource: “percentage points” labels absolute share changes correctly, and “total mass collected” identifies the missing denominator. Refinement: retain share/proportion language consistently rather than describing composting itself as common without its waste-mass context.

Grammatical range and accuracy: “whereas the landfill proportion decreased by 40 points” correctly contrasts two complete changes. Refinement: check that the pronoun “They” in the final paragraph unambiguously refers to the figures if paragraphs are edited.
explanation.ru:
Иллюстративный ИИ-образец; band не выставляется.

Выполнение задания: «lost its dominant position as recycling expanded» обозначает главный сдвиг; «25% each» верно описывает конечное равенство. Уточнение: при необходимости полезного отношения прямо сравните конечную переработку с начальной — в два с половиной раза больше.

Связность: «Five years later» и «By 2024» ведут хронологическую структуру, а обзор сохраняет общую картину. Уточнение: конечное ограничение можно включить в абзац деталей, уменьшив отдельное заключение.

Лексика: «percentage points» правильно обозначает абсолютные изменения долей, «total mass collected» — отсутствующий знаменатель. Уточнение: последовательно сохраняйте язык долей, не называя компостирование распространённым без контекста массы отходов.

Грамматика: «whereas the landfill proportion decreased by 40 points» верно противопоставляет полные изменения. Уточнение: при редактировании абзацев проверьте, что финальное «They» однозначно относится к числам.

chart.title: Household waste treatment in fictional Marden Borough

exercises.sampleAnswer:
The chart presents the distribution of collected household waste among three treatment routes in Marden Borough in 2014, 2019 and 2024. Overall, landfill lost its dominant position as recycling expanded. Composting also became more common and accounted for the same share as landfill by the final year.

In 2014, landfill received 65% of the collected waste, considerably more than the combined recycling and composting share of 35%. Recycling represented one fifth of the total, while composting accounted for the remaining 15%. Five years later, landfill had fallen to 45%, but it was still the largest individual category. Recycling and composting had reached 35% and 20%, respectively.

By 2024, half of the collected waste was recycled. The other half was divided equally between landfill and composting, at 25% each. The recycling share therefore increased by 30 percentage points across the period, whereas the landfill proportion decreased by 40 points. Composting rose more gradually, gaining 5 points in each interval.

These figures show a substantial change in how the collected waste was treated. They do not show the total mass collected, so the decline in landfill's share cannot establish how many tonnes stopped going to landfill.

exercises.prompt: Academic Task 1: The chart compares mean daily bicycle rentals on weekdays and weekend days at fictional Kelm Hire in four months of 2024. Task achievement: Describe both series peaking in July and weekend means exceeding weekday means in every month shown. The gap is widest in July at 100 rentals per day.

Coherence and cohesion: Compare the shared seasonal shape first, then contrast gaps and endpoint levels rather than listing eight values.

Lexical resource: Keep mean daily rentals in the wording. Weekend days is a day category, not the sum of all rentals across a weekend.

Grammatical range and accuracy: Use prepositions accurately: peaked at 260 in July and fell to 180 by October. Do not use future tense for 2024 observations.

exercises.prompt: Academic Task 1: The chart shows mean depot-to-depot delivery times for comparable standard consignments sent by road, rail and coastal ship in a fictional logistics network in 2012, 2018 and 2024. Summarise the main features and make relevant comparisons. Write at least 150 words in about 20 minutes. All values are fictional hours per delivery. They exclude time before dispatch and after arrival.

explanation.en:
Task achievement: Identify declining durations for all three modes, road as shortest throughout and coastal ship as longest. Shipping has the largest absolute reduction, 10 hours; road–rail difference narrows from 6 to 2 hours.

Coherence and cohesion: Group the shared downward trend before comparing initial and final gaps. Explain that lower duration represents faster delivery without describing a falling speed.

Lexical resource: Distinguish duration from speed and end-to-end customer waiting time. Use shortened by and shortened to with the correct figures.

Grammatical range and accuracy: Write parallel comparisons across modes and preserve hours after quantities. Check than after shorter.

This is formative practice guidance; no official band is assigned.
explanation.ru:
Выполнение задания: Укажите сокращение длительности всех способов, дорогу как самую быструю и судно как самое медленное. У судна крупнейшее абсолютное сокращение — 10 часов; разрыв дороги и рельсов сужается с 6 до 2 часов.

Связность и организация: Сначала объедините общий нисходящий тренд, затем начальные и конечные разрывы. Меньшая длительность означает более быструю доставку, а не снижение скорости.

Лексика: Отличайте длительность от скорости и полного ожидания клиента. Используйте shortened by и shortened to с верными числами.

Грамматический диапазон и точность: Стройте параллельные сравнения способов и сохраняйте hours после количеств. Проверьте than после shorter.

Это тренировочные рекомендации; официальный band не выставляется.

exercises.prompt: Academic Task 1: The chart shows enrolments and successful completions for four courses at fictional Vesta Adult College in 2024. Summarise the main features and make relevant comparisons. Write at least 150 words in about 20 minutes. All figures are fictional numbers of course enrolments. Completions are a subset of enrolments in each course; a learner may enrol in more than one course.

explanation.en:
Illustrative AI-authored sample; no band assigned.

Task achievement: “shared the highest completion rate despite their different sizes” recognises the 108/120 = 72/80 = 90% comparison. “360 enrolment records and 302 completion records” sums the supplied counts correctly. Refinement: if brevity is needed, prioritise the rate comparison over the aggregate totals.

Coherence and cohesion: “However” introduces the difference between size and success rate, which later paragraphs explain. Refinement: grouping both 90% courses together earlier would reduce movement between counting and proportion comparisons.

Lexical resource: “enrolment records” avoids equating enrolments with distinct people; “numerical gap” distinguishes a count difference from a rate. Refinement: specify non-completion only when describing the gap, rather than implying reasons such as failure or withdrawal that are not provided.

Grammatical range and accuracy: “of which 108 ended in successful completion” supplies a controlled relative structure. Refinement: preserve the plural verb after “Both this course and computing” when editing; vary sentence openings without dropping the compared category.
explanation.ru:
Иллюстративный ИИ-образец; band не выставляется.

Выполнение задания: «shared the highest completion rate despite their different sizes» отражает 108/120 = 72/80 = 90%. «360 enrolment records and 302 completion records» верно суммирует данные. Уточнение: при сокращении отдайте приоритет сравнению долей перед общими суммами.

Связность: «However» вводит различие размера и доли завершения, раскрытое далее. Уточнение: более раннее объединение обоих курсов с 90% уменьшило бы переходы между количествами и долями.

Лексика: «enrolment records» не приравнивает записи к разным людям; «numerical gap» отличает разность количеств от доли. Уточнение: описывайте лишь незавершение, не подразумевая неизвестные причины вроде провала или отказа.

Грамматика: «of which 108 ended in successful completion» даёт точную относительную конструкцию. Уточнение: при редактировании сохраните множественное число после «Both this course and computing»; меняйте начала предложений, не теряя сравниваемую категорию.

hints.en: Compare absolute counts first; then divide completed by enrolled for each course.
hints.ru: Сначала сравните количества; затем разделите завершения на записи каждого курса.

hints.en: Look for two different-sized courses with the same completion proportion.
hints.ru: Найдите два курса разных размеров с одинаковой долей завершения.

typicalErrors.en: Calling 108 completions a 108% completion rate.
typicalErrors.ru: Обозначение 108 завершений как 108% завершения.

typicalErrors.en: Assuming all enrolment records represent different people.
typicalErrors.ru: Предположение, что все записи принадлежат разным людям.

typicalErrors.en: Treating the largest number completed as proof of the uniquely highest rate.
typicalErrors.ru: Принятие крупнейшего числа завершений за доказательство единственной высшей доли.

criteria.ru: Выполнение задания: Назовите информатику крупнейшей, садоводство наименьшим по обоим числам. У информатики и учёта одинаковая высшая доля завершения 90% при разных числах; садоводство ниже всех — 70%.

criteria.ru: Лексика: Различайте enrolments, completions и completion rate. Сумма записей не обязательно равна числу разных учащихся.

criteria.en: Grammatical range and accuracy: Use of in 108 of 120 and agreement with courses versus the course. Check numerical comparisons for complete clauses.
criteria.ru: Грамматический диапазон и точность: Используйте of в 108 of 120 и согласование с courses и the course. Проверяйте полноту предложений с числовыми сравнениями.

chart.title: Course enrolments and completions at fictional Vesta Adult College

exercises.sampleAnswer:
The chart compares enrolment and completion records for four courses at Vesta Adult College in 2024. Overall, basic computing had the largest numbers enrolled and completing, whereas gardening had the smallest. However, basic computing and bookkeeping shared the highest completion rate despite their different sizes.

Basic computing attracted 120 enrolments, of which 108 ended in successful completion. Languages ranked second by enrolment, with 100 records, but only 80 completions. The language course therefore had the largest numerical gap between the two measures, at 20, compared with 12 for computing.

Bookkeeping recorded 80 enrolments and 72 completions. Both this course and computing consequently achieved a completion rate of 90%. The corresponding proportion for languages was lower, at 80%. Gardening was smaller than the other courses on both measures, with 60 enrolments and 42 completions, equivalent to a 70% completion rate.

Across all four courses, there were 360 enrolment records and 302 completion records. These totals describe participation in courses rather than the number of distinct people at the college, because a learner could enrol in more than one subject. The comparison therefore distinguishes the volume of course activity from the proportion of enrolments successfully completed.

exercises.prompt: Academic Task 1: The chart compares the shares of booked room-hours used for arts, sports and study activities at fictional Orven Community Centre in 2010 and 2025. Summarise the main features and make relevant comparisons. Write at least 150 words in about 20 minutes. All values are fictional percentages of total booked room-hours. These three activities account for all bookings in the dataset; total booked hours are not given.

explanation.en:
Task achievement: State that study replaced sports as the largest share. Sports halved from 50% to 25%; arts and study both rose. Describe distribution without claiming a change in total bookings.

Coherence and cohesion: Separate the changed ranking from detailed comparisons. Compare study’s 15-point gain with arts’ 10-point gain and sports’ 25-point decline.

Lexical resource: Retain booked room-hours as the denominator. Halved is accurate for the sports share, not necessarily the absolute hours of sport.

Grammatical range and accuracy: Use comparative structures and past tense consistently; check the share of sports was rather than were.

This is formative practice guidance; no official band is assigned.
explanation.ru:
Выполнение задания: Укажите, что учёба сменила спорт как крупнейшую долю. Спорт сократился вдвое с 50% до 25%; искусство и учёба выросли. Описывайте распределение без утверждения об изменении общей загрузки.

Связность и организация: Отделите смену мест от подробных сравнений. Сопоставьте рост учёбы на 15 пунктов, искусства на 10 и падение спорта на 25.

Лексика: Сохраняйте забронированные часы помещений как знаменатель. Halved верно для доли спорта, но не обязательно для абсолютных часов.

Грамматический диапазон и точность: Последовательно используйте сравнения и прошедшее время; проверьте the share of sports was, а не were.

Это тренировочные рекомендации; официальный band не выставляется.

hints.en: Use both percentage-point changes and one accurate ratio, while preserving the denominator.
hints.ru: Используйте изменения в пунктах и одно точное отношение, сохраняя знаменатель.

exercises.prompt: Academic Task 1: The chart shows stored water volume in the East and West reservoirs of fictional Taren District from May to September 2024. Summarise the main features and make relevant comparisons. Write at least 150 words in about 20 minutes. All values are fictional millions of cubic metres of stored water, measured at the same scheduled point in each month. Reservoir capacities and water inflows are not provided.

explanation.en:
Task achievement: Describe both reservoirs falling to August lows and recovering in September. East starts higher but falls below West in August and remains lower in September; its net loss is larger.

Coherence and cohesion: Group the shared pattern in an overview, then compare the larger East changes and the ranking reversal. Use the first observed reversal rather than inventing an exact crossing date.

Lexical resource: Describe stored volume, not percentage fullness or consumption. Fell by 35 million cubic metres over the whole period applies to East.

Grammatical range and accuracy: Use lower than for comparisons and fell to for minima. Keep the time reference of by August distinct from in September.

This is formative practice guidance; no official band is assigned.
explanation.ru:
Выполнение задания: Опишите снижение обоих водохранилищ до августовских минимумов и восстановление в сентябре. Восточное начинает выше, но в августе становится ниже западного и остаётся ниже в сентябре; его итоговая потеря больше.

Связность и организация: Объедините общий рисунок в обзоре, затем сравните более крупные изменения восточного и смену лидера. Используйте первую наблюдаемую смену, не выдумывая точную дату пересечения.

Лексика: Описывайте запас объёма, а не процент наполнения или потребление. Падение на 35 миллионов кубометров за весь период относится к восточному.

Грамматический диапазон и точность: Используйте lower than для сравнения и fell to для минимумов. Различайте временные отсылки by August и in September.

Это тренировочные рекомендации; официальный band не выставляется.

hints.en: Find each minimum and identify the first shown month with West above East.
hints.ru: Найдите минимум каждого ряда и первый показанный месяц, где западное выше восточного.

hints.en: Compare net changes, then explain the September recovery without inventing its cause.
hints.ru: Сравните итоговые изменения, затем опишите сентябрьское восстановление без выдуманной причины.

typicalErrors.en: Calling the values percentages of reservoir capacity.
typicalErrors.ru: Обозначение значений как процентов вместимости.

typicalErrors.en: Treating the volume decline as an exact measure of consumption without inflow data.
typicalErrors.ru: Принятие снижения запаса за точное потребление без данных притока.

typicalErrors.en: Claiming continuous decline despite the September recovery.
typicalErrors.ru: Заявление о непрерывном снижении при сентябрьском восстановлении.

exercises.prompt: Short Academic Task 2 diagnostic: Some employers allow staff to choose their starting and finishing times. Others require the same fixed hours for everyone. Discuss both approaches and give your own opinion about when flexibility is appropriate. Write at least 120 words in about 8 minutes. This is an abbreviated skill probe; a full Task 2 response requires at least 250 words. Give reasons and a relevant example; no specialist knowledge is required.

explanation.en:
Task response: Explain one benefit of flexibility and one reason for shared hours, then state a position that addresses when each is appropriate. Any reasoned view is acceptable.

Coherence and cohesion: Give each approach a distinct role in the argument. Connect your condition for flexibility to the reason you gave, rather than adding an unrelated compromise.

Lexical resource: Use working hours, availability and coordination precisely. Flexible hours do not necessarily mean fewer hours or working from home.

Grammatical range and accuracy: Use conditional clauses to state limits, such as if customers need continuous cover. Check plural staff members and agreement.

This is formative practice guidance; no official band is assigned.
explanation.ru:
Раскрытие задачи: Объясните пользу гибкости и одну причину общего расписания, затем укажите, когда уместен каждый подход. Допустима любая обоснованная позиция.

Связность и организация: Отведите каждому подходу отдельную роль. Свяжите условие гибкости с приведённой причиной вместо несвязанного компромисса.

Лексика: Точно используйте working hours, availability и coordination. Гибкие часы не обязательно означают меньше работы или работу из дома.

Грамматический диапазон и точность: Используйте условные придаточные для ограничений, например if customers need continuous cover. Проверьте staff members и согласование.

Это тренировочные рекомендации; официальный band не выставляется.

hints.en: Choose one individual benefit and one coordination need before deciding your position.
hints.ru: До выбора позиции определите личную пользу и потребность в координации.

hints.en: Use a concrete contrast, such as an independent task versus a shared service desk.
hints.ru: Используйте конкретный контраст: самостоятельная задача и общая стойка обслуживания.

typicalErrors.en: Giving an opinion without discussing both approaches.
typicalErrors.ru: Мнение без обсуждения обоих подходов.

exercises.prompt: Academic Task 2: A university is considering making a supervised work placement a compulsory part of every undergraduate degree. Do the advantages of this policy outweigh the disadvantages? Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words in about 40 minutes. You may use clearly illustrative examples rather than research statistics.

explanation.en:
Illustrative AI-authored sample; no band assigned.

Task response: “the disadvantages of a universal requirement outweigh its advantages” answers the question directly. The design-student example explains a benefit, while quality and access support the judgment. Refinement: clarify how the proposed external project would receive equivalent supervision, so the alternative meets the same educational standard.

Coherence and cohesion: “However, the quality of that experience is crucial” turns from a developed benefit to a limiting condition; “Access creates another difficulty” adds a distinct objection. Refinement: link the two objections explicitly as conditions the university must satisfy, reducing the impression of a list.

Lexical resource: “educational value” and “credible alternatives” fit the argument without overstating outcomes. Refinement: replace one repeated “requirement” with a precise reference such as this policy, provided the referent stays clear.

Grammatical range and accuracy: “If universities must find a position for every student” introduces a complete conditional argument, while “may be unable to travel” appropriately limits the access claim. Refinement: shorten a long conditional sentence if its main clause becomes difficult to follow when read aloud.
explanation.ru:
Иллюстративный ИИ-образец; band не выставляется.

Раскрытие задачи: «the disadvantages of a universal requirement outweigh its advantages» прямо отвечает на вопрос. Пример студента-дизайнера объясняет пользу; качество и доступ поддерживают вывод. Уточнение: объясните равноценный надзор за внешним проектом, чтобы альтернатива соответствовала тому же учебному стандарту.

Связность: «However, the quality of that experience is crucial» переводит развитую пользу к условию; «Access creates another difficulty» добавляет отдельное возражение. Уточнение: явно свяжите возражения как условия для университета, уменьшая впечатление списка.

Лексика: «educational value» и «credible alternatives» соответствуют доводу без завышения результатов. Уточнение: замените один повтор requirement точной отсылкой this policy, сохраняя ясный референт.

Грамматика: «If universities must find a position for every student» вводит полное условное рассуждение; «may be unable to travel» уместно ограничивает заявление о доступе. Уточнение: сократите длинное условное предложение, если его главную часть трудно воспринимать вслух.

hints.en: Focus on compulsory and every degree: these words create the main trade-off.
hints.ru: Сосредоточьтесь на compulsory и every degree: они создают главный компромисс.

hints.en: Compare one concrete learning benefit with one access or academic-fit problem, then weigh them.
hints.ru: Сопоставьте конкретную учебную пользу с проблемой доступа или соответствия программе, затем взвесьте их.

typicalErrors.en: Listing advantages and disadvantages without deciding which outweighs the other.
typicalErrors.ru: Перечисление преимуществ и недостатков без решения, что перевешивает.

typicalErrors.en: Ignoring differences between disciplines or students’ access to placements.
typicalErrors.ru: Игнорирование различий дисциплин или доступа студентов к практике.

typicalErrors.en: Presenting invented employment percentages as real evidence.
typicalErrors.ru: Представление выдуманных процентов занятости как реальных доказательств.
